titleStmt.title: Hippiatrica Cantabrigiensia; or, The Cambridge Hippiatrica

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un helleniste) a partir du texte grec deja present dans le corpus zoomathia sous zoo80/1g (Hippiatrica Cantabrigiensia, TLG 0738, compilation byzantine de medecine veterinaire equine transmise sous le nom collectif de plusieurs auteurs anciens cites nommement dans le texte meme : Apsyrtus, Hierocles, Pelagonius, Africanus, Theomnestus, Simon d'Athenes, Oribasius, entre autres). Le decoupage en 384 unites de traduction reprend fidelement, dans l'ordre du document, la structure de divisions du fichier source (types book/chapter/section/subsection/treatise/poem/strophe et leurs numeros n, lesquels renvoient au systeme de numerotation comparative de l'edition critique moderne recoupant plusieurs temoins manuscrits — Cantabrigiensis, Berolinensis, Parisina — et ne correspondent donc pas a une numerotation continue simple). Les numeros de renvoi de l'apparat comparatif qui apparaissaient comme paragraphes autonomes dans le texte source (par ex. "14.4.1", "26.2.10") ont ete silencieusement retires car ce sont des reperes d'edition, non du texte a proprement parler ; les quatre unites du decoupage source qui ne contenaient plus que de tels reperes une fois ce nettoyage effectue (aucun texte reel) ont ete omises de la traduction. Les lacunes du manuscrit unique (signalees dans le texte source par des asterisques) sont rendues par la mention explicite "[lacuna]" ou "[the manuscript breaks off here, unfinished]" plutot que comblees par conjecture ; le texte s'acheve d'ailleurs, comme le temoin manuscrit source lui-meme, sur une recette interrompue en son debut ("Skeuasia dia pikras. ***"). Ce texte est une compilation pharmacologique et hippiatrique tres dense (mesures grecques/byzantines rendues en anglais courant, non converties : litra/"pound", ounce/oungia, "carat"/keration, "hexagion"), melangeant recettes veterinaires, notes d'anatomie et de conformation du cheval, et quelques formules magiques ou charmes d'origine chretienne tardive caracteristiques des couches byzantines de la compilation. Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un helleniste specialiste de medecine veterinaire antique avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte grec deja present dans le corpus sous zoo80/1g.

div.p: A horse becomes healthy by eating grain and drinking wine; but if it does not become so — eating grain, yet not drinking wine — it is heavy and weak.
On arthritic glanders.
For dry glanders: peony is suited to dry glanders,
which occurs for the most part when you have not forestalled it by treating the animal with the proper remedies in time. It arises in one case from the head, in another from the great windpipe.
It is called ‘dry’ because the same cough besets it, just as in animals that have never come to suppuration.

You will recognize the difference from the signs: the horse behaves as though weighed down and shrinks backward, avoiding its place in line, and it brings up greenish, foul matter that has not yet come to suppuration.
Let us treat this, then, by pouring peony with a pint and an ounce of fresh water into the nostrils, and let us also apply a straight cautery to the head itself.
For moist glanders. If one of the draught animals is troubled by moist glanders, it coughs violently, so that its whole body is strained, and swellings appear beneath the tongue,
and when it coughs, it brings up through the nostrils pus that is thick and the color of a quince.
Hence it seems to me that ‘malis’ [glanders] is named from this very color: for in the Doric dialect quince-yellow (mēlinon) is called malinon.
It occurs especially when there is a sudden change of air and water, from frost or snow, or again from warm air suddenly turning cold.
Let us treat it thus: we draw blood from the sinew above the breastbone, and anoint the head with vinegar and oil, or with wine and oil if it comes from cold, and let us instill—

—the juice of heliotrope, two pounds and three ounces, together with a little opium and niter, pouring it with vinegar through both nostrils. This both draws out the pus and clears the glanders. Or: seed of chaste-tree (which is called ‘lygaia’), nine ounces; myrrh, nine carats; saffron, the same; bitter almonds, fifteen; grind both together, pour on two ounces two hexagia of vinegar and nine ounces of oil, warm it, and pour it in through the mouth.

Another inhalant to break up the glanders through the nostrils; it also helps those with lung trouble. Grind and sift through a fine sieve one ounce of white soapwort, and blow it into the nostrils through a reed, nine carats’ worth: for it strongly provokes sneezing and draws off much phlegm. But if, after this is applied, the disease grows worse, draw blood from the neck and anoint and cover it. The root of cyclamen, too, poured in with old wine, is good, until the animal is purged. And when it seems to be doing well, but is still troubled by coughing, grind pure frankincense well with sweet wine and pour it in, until it recovers.

For animals troubled in the windpipe and lungs, and suffering some injury from these, take away the chaff and dry fodder; use alfalfa instead, or sprinkle the dry fodder with must before giving it, and give soaked barley too, mixing in linseed with it. The leaves of radishes given to eat are also good.
On subcutaneous glanders. We recognize this disease by the foul-smelling pus discharged through the nostrils

—together with coughing and wasting of the body, and often too the skin bursts open wherever it happens on the body, and pus-filled sores break out. Hence this glanders too seems to be called ‘subcutaneous.’ Its treatment is nourishing food, which changes the acrid and ill-humored matter in the moist parts of the body.

Take a suckling puppy, slaughter it, singe off the hair, clean and wash the inner parts well, and boil it with vetch-gruel, pouring on ten pints of rainwater or spring water, adding a little niter. Boil until it is reduced by half, then strain and mix in a handful of barley meal and eighteen carats of unfired sulphur (that is, brimstone). Then grind it together, pour in wine equal to the broth, and give this as a drench through the mouth every third day — for this is ‘the remedy given every other day.’ Or boil a cock and use the broth likewise, and wash with warm water. Let it have food of every kind, and feed it as much as it will take. But also give it dried stag’s pizzle, pounded, mixed with salt, to eat.

If a foal develops glanders while still nursing. Give a drench of soda, wine, and oil for three days, and it will stop. And if the foal also catches quinsy, make a plaster of linseed, honey, and oil, and apply it to the throat with a cloth, and it will break open the inner swelling.

Signs and treatment of renal glanders. The hind legs drag, the fetlocks give way, it eats much yet grows thin. Bleed it from the forelegs at first. But if you delay and do not bleed it, then instead lay it down—

—and cauterize below, on the buttocks and flanks, in the shape of a lambda, and drench the burns with brine and water. Then take one and a half ounces each of tragacanth gum and honey, oak-gall, cardamom, spikenard leaf, and pepper, one ounce each [and four ounces of honey], ten ounces of white wine; grind fine and give as a drench for three days, and it will be cured.

Tiberius’s remedy for glanders. Pound the fresh root of the wild cucumber (that is, the wild gourd), press out the juice, and give it as a drench, or bind it on as an amulet. Or boil vetch-gruel with marjoram and garlic until it becomes a broth, strain the juice, mix in goat fat, and boil until it dissolves, then give it warm as a drench. Or grind two ounces two hexagia of white sesame with goat’s milk, warm it, and use. Or one and a half ounces of tragacanth, and so on; or myrrh from the Troglodyte country, and so on.
Another remedy. Bleed from the neck, add twenty ounces of dry wine and the same of oil, half an ounce of pomegranate rind ground fine, and knead it with honey and give it to chew for three days.

For both kinds of glanders. Dry and grind the dung of leopard, bear, and camel, and fumigate first the head, then the belly down to the groins, then the whole body. Also give to drink the seed of the cucumber (that is, melon seed) with niter. Then, after washing it in the sea, lead it into its stall, having first blown wine and oil warm over its whole body.
For moist glanders. Grind garlic, add butter and honey, and plenty of cedar-resin; warm it and pour it in through both the nostrils and the mouth, or bind on beaver-skin to each—
—animal, and give each animal a drench of unmixed wine with milk, six ounces to each.
A powerful remedy. This has been confirmed by experience.

The root of black hellebore, and so on. Or burn a whole pine-cone, add nine sprigs of bramble-heads, one pound of honey, five hexagia of butter, ten ounces of old wine; pound and grind it, and give as a drench through the mouth.
A fumigation for glanders. Fumigate with pine-cone and peony, with the head covered.

For every kind of glanders. The plant called ‘black-wheat’ [melampyron], and so on; or vetch, or bean, and so on; or the juice of wild cucumber root, two eggs, with common oil, drenched warm through the nostrils. But first anoint the loins and the back.

For dry glanders. One part of the juice of wild cucumber root, and so on; anoint also the feet with scraped verdigris mixed with enough vinegar. Or pour twelve carats of ground mulberry root with warm wine through the nostrils.
A nasal remedy of Hippocrates for arthritic glanders. Burnt niter, soapwort, and so on.

Another way. Take nightshade seed and the little maiden-herb called mercury [linozostis], grind vigorously, pouring on ten ounces of water, until it becomes smooth and has the thickness of milk. Then strain it and mix in thirteen and a half ounces of honey, ten ounces of white wine, one ounce of unripe-olive oil, and drench through both nostrils.
Another way. One ounce each of pepper and black cummin, six ounces each of coriander and marjoram, one ounce of spurge; blow the ground powder into the nostrils, and drench the head with warm oil.
If it discharges foul-smelling moisture through the nostrils. [lacuna in the manuscript]
On the horse afflicted with elephantiasis.
By Africanus. The liver of the land hedgehog, dried in the sun and given to drink with wine, cures horses afflicted with elephantiasis.

An ointment for the same. One ounce each of wild raisins, myrrh, aloe, and alum; one and a half ounces each of orpiment and mastic; seven hexagia of frankincense; two ounces of Gangra salt; two ounces of goat fat; four ounces of the bark of wild fig-tree root. Boil it all with vinegar until the vinegar disappears, then grind the bark, add one ounce of wax and four ounces of oil, combine both and boil until dissolved, and use.

Another. One ounce each of liquid pitch, unfired sulphur, niter, and wax; one and a half ounces of turpentine; three ounces of sponge-stone [pumice]; pound and sift the dry ingredients, melt the meltable ones and combine, and use, letting it sit for three days. Or grind together one ounce each of celandine, barley meal, and white lead, and take it up in the first runnings of soap-lye, called ‘proteios’ broth, and use. Or pound and sift equal parts of litharge and unfired sulphur, combine in squill vinegar, and grind for a long time until it becomes like water; then add bay oil and walnut oil, warm it, and use.

For ‘stumbling,’ that is, the sacred disease [i.e. epilepsy]. The affliction of stumbling often occurs from exhaustion, sometimes from cold, sometimes from heat, and sometimes even from food. It will be recognized if it shows these signs: it throws itself down, stretches out, then curls up again, and each leg is sometimes extended, sometimes drawn in, and, dragging itself along the ground by the mouth, it circles round, and though it wants—

—to get up, the horse is prevented. Give, then, a drench of opopanax dissolved in warm mixed wine, or clematis-vine birthwort, or roasted, pounded cumin. When it does get up, let it be walked about and rubbed down with wine and oil. While it lies on the ground, set food and drink beside it, as the occasion allows; for even if it rises, it staggers sideways as it walks. Often the affliction persists for several days. Among men this is called the ‘sacred disease’ [epilepsy].

Another. Drench through the right nostril with four and a half hexagia of finely ground niter, two ounces of warm water, and four and a half hexagia of oil, until it shows signs of recovering. It is also said that scraping dried stag’s pizzle into fine shreds, mixing it with salt, and giving it to the horse to eat, helps. Others think it best to open the temporal and neck veins and shut the animal in a dark place, anointing the temples and nostrils with ground rue mixed with vinegar and oil. Or mix turtle’s blood, vinegar, and wine, five ounces each, with eighteen carats of Cyrenaic sap [silphium], and pour it in through the nostrils.

Another treatment. It is understood that in the horse the sacred disease shows itself especially through the eyes: for the eyes are seen to look like unfired sulphur, and appear filled with bile. Indeed this disease for the most part arises from an excess of bile. It is treated thus: pound the root of wild spartium and put it into ten pints of water and boil until reduced to a third. Pour this through the nostrils of the horse, letting the horse’s head hang up for a long while. But if greater necessity demands it, add four and a half ounces of the finest fish-sauce to the drink. And if the very—
—joints stiffen, and so on.
Another effective remedy. Two and a half ounces of white soda, cimolian earth,
one and a half hexagia each of black cummin, and of bryony (that is, white vine)
root, the same amount; of sea-anemone (which is called ‘arteonion’), two and a half ounces,
four and a half ounces of unfired sulphur, and the root of white chamaeleon-thistle; grind it all
and sprinkle it on.
Pelagonius, against the plague.
On the lung, on lung-rupture, and
on pneumonia.
On the pneumonic horse. The horse with pneumonia is recognized by the following:
its neck grows thin, and
it digests poorly at the onset and loses its appetite. As the affliction persists,
it discharges mucous humors, and through the mouth or
the nostrils it casts out foam streaked with blood; it also sweats about the
armpits, with fever, and once the peritoneum has been drawn up, it readily
succumbs, unless the disease is forestalled. Give it as a drench
cucumber and niter with sweet, chilled wine. There are three
kinds of lung affliction: ‘under-the-spleen’ pneumonic, [true] pneumonic, and ‘lung-bound’ [pain in the belly]. In these, then, at
the outset, apply the phlebotomy. Then make a gruel from fine
wheat flour, boil it with marjoram and honey, and give as a drench; or
roast and grind wolf’s liver and give as a drench with one pound
of wine.
On the lung. The pneumonic horse shows the sign
of casting out foam. Give a drench of water and honey, and steam
its armpits ten or twelve times, to relax the lung,
and draw blood from the neck. And as you watch
the animal, draw blood again from the armpits.
—a little pig, and so on; or from wheat leaven, and so on; or garlic, and so on; or boil a pig’s ham with water until it takes on the consistency of glue. Give this as a drench with a horn.

Another remarkable remedy for the same. Spiced wine, and so on; or seven worms, and so on; or give freshly drawn goat’s milk a second time as a drench through the mouth. But also give fresh, warm pig’s fat together with the milk.
On barley-surfeit [laminitis from overeating barley].
Apsyrtus to Ammonius, and so on; or henbane, and so on; or grind a swallow’s nest with water and give it to drink, or give six ounces of leek juice to drink.

Another way. When the barley-surfeit reaches the feet, it is helpful to bleed from the veins between the pasterns, and the next day to poultice with bran and vinegar, so as to break down the harm. Also mix as much blood of a suckling piglet as makes a mixture with an equal amount of wine, and give as a drench through the mouth. Let it walk about and be exercised, and it will be healthy. This too is excellent to do at once: three ounces of fluff [wool-down], enough sharp vinegar, one ounce of rosin; mix and boil, and anoint from the fetlocks to the knees.
If a horse eats wheat contrary to its nature. Mix greasy wool with warm water and a little honey, press it out, and give it to drink. If it will not drink, pour it in through the mouth.
And draw blood from the chest, and let it walk about a little. A drench given through the mouth is also necessary.
On phlebotomy.
On disturbing, that is, excessive, blood.

An animal suffering from excess blood shows these signs: the eyes swell, the body and neck are cold, a gloominess comes over it, and it lies down with difficulty. It will be healed in this way: it will be kept from food and drink, and it will be given an abundance of sleep and soft bedding. Then, from the jugular vein — that is, the principal vein — as much blood as the case requires will be drawn. Nor should the treatment by drenching be neglected: therefore a full spoonful of germander and centaury with roses and niter, all finely sifted in equal parts, is poured into the mouth with half a pint of warm water. This purges and heals the excess moisture and blood and all the diseases attending it.

A styptic powder. Grind oak-galls and mix in copper sulfate, deer hair, and hare hair, and apply. Riding-donkeys, however, should be bled around the calends of March, before breeding begins, and oxen too three days before they are due to be turned out to pasture, above the nose.

Another way. Take a pledget soaked in frankincense manna and lay it on the place, and put on a wad wetted with wine. Then lay wool over it and bind it up thus. The next day let the place be soaked with wine-and-oil while the bandages remain on, and do this for three or four days. Then let it be undone and treated with the usual treatment for wounds.
On diseases of the eyes.
A plaster for cataracts. Divine wisdom devised this too, so that, should the need ever arise, neither—
—should the medical matter drawn down by the sclerotic have to be dislodged,
nor should an instrument be needed to cut open the membrane of the eye.
But the iron-colored cataract is to be excluded from
this treatment; use instead: one ounce of magnetic stone [magnetite], half an ounce of Alexandrian niter, and as much turpentine as is needed to make a plaster.

Apply this plaster from the brow down to below the cheekbone, taking care in the middle of the plaster to leave the eyes free, so that the lids can still move, and remove and re-press it fairly often.

For a fistula of the eye. Split a dry lupine-cake down the middle, smear it with saliva, and apply it. Do this repeatedly and you will cure it. Or chop rue fine, mix it with human dung, and apply it to the place.

Or pound and sift lupine-cakes, and knead together Greek cumin, pure white myrrh, the juice of rue, and the juice of peach leaves with very sharp vinegar, and, having made it into a plaster, apply it.
Or knead the juice of rue with galbanum and apply it twice a day. Attention must be paid to the sensitivity or insensitivity of the eye being treated;
for eyes that by nature have eyelashes full of blood, and those that are grey-blue, cannot bear at all the astringency of eye-salves.
Hence one must apply to these remedies that are more watery and non-biting.

The eye-salve called ‘one-day,’ because it heals from a single application, is also effective against chronic and stubborn conditions, especially where the eyelids have become rough. Use it with water. If—

—the inflammation is severe, drench it with egg white as well. It is made thus: three ounces each of cadmia and gum, blue vitriol, roasted chalcitis, opium, and honey one and a half ounces, twenty-one grains of pepper, and enough water.

Another way — Antoninus’s — which fills in pits, cleans scars, and very effectively drives back inflammations: three ounces each of cadmia and white lead, two ounces one and a half hexagia of acacia gum, opium the same, gum, tragacanth, and starch one ounce eighteen carats each, myrrh two hexagia six carats, copper one hexagion three carats, saffron the same; grind these in water and use.

For fistula of the eye. These are cured by applying Gallic soap, or dried pig’s gall, or golden hen’s droppings ground with chalk to the consistency of a plaster and applied repeatedly; or fresh cheese made from goat’s milk applied to the wound twice a day, for it cleanses, builds flesh, and closes the scar. And after the fistula has burst, apply the pith found inside the reed at the joints. It is a tested remedy.

An eye-remedy of Africanus. The swallow carries the juice of a certain herb, from which, if a drop falls to earth, another herb grows from the drop, named after the bird that dropped it. It also grows if the chicks, having partaken of it, excrete it to the ground. This is a marvelous and effective remedy for dim sight; it gradually thins away the white films caused by wounds and restores the eye to its unaffected form. But the herb produced from the droppings is less potent, and less successful.

—it also drives away grey-blue eyes when rubbed in. And its dust with water does everything the earlier remedy did. For if anyone were fortunate enough to gather the first-found herb, it would open even blind eyes.

Two stones found in the bellies of chicks, when cut open with a sharp reed [for they are found in only one], one white and one black, of a white dove that has been sacrificed and named after Aphrodite, are set in a gold necklace and ward off every eye-disease. [Cutting open the spring chicks, you will find stones in the belly, of which one is speckled, the other plain. Before it touches the ground, bind it in the skin of a fawn or calf against the great disease (epilepsy), and you will perhaps cure it, but in any case you will lessen the epilepsy.] One must cut them open for this purpose at the beginning of the month, taking them as it waxes.

They say that partridge gall mixed with Attic honey cures dim sight and cataract; and this is evident to many. And the eyes of a vulture, bound in a clean linen cloth and applied to the eyes daily, do not allow dim sight to occur, nor cataract to form. And an eye of the vulture tied up in dog-skin does not allow eye-inflammation. Its gall, smeared on with the juice of horehound and Attic honey, removes every dimness and mist of the eyes, and does not allow incipient cataracts to form.
The eyes of a living frog, removed and, wrapped in a linen rag, worn on the left arm or the neck, keep the eyes free from disease—
—and if you bind it on someone in pain, you will release the affliction. The frog itself must be released where it was caught. Its gall too is smeared on for sharp sight and cataract.

Nothing is better than this for sharpness of sight: make eye-salves from ivy root, put them in a box of red copper together with the urine of an infant boy, tie it up securely, and bury it in horse dung for forty days. Then take it out, rub it on a whetstone, and make eye-salves with the liquid that has formed, and you will marvel at its effect; it also stops incipient cataracts.
For cataract. Smear on eagle’s gall.
For dim sight. Take up ammoniac gum with the urine of an uncorrupted boy, and use.

For painless ophthalmia, tested by experience. Three ounces of good Cimolian earth, three ounces of purslane juice; mix both and apply to the eye, and when it has dried, remove it, and grind it again with purslane juice and re-anoint.

For a discharge of the eye. Grind saffron with woman’s milk and smear it on; or grind a donkey’s first-shed tooth and smear it on with egg white. Or take the ash gathered from bronze-workers’ forges, grind it with saffron and egg, and apply it from temple to temple with a wad of lint. Or take a root of rue in the left hand and tie it on, saying: ‘I take you away from the pain of the eye of this horse called so-and-so.’ Or knead barley flour, lime, and saffron with honey, and spread it on the forehead.
For a flux of the eye. Put cock’s gall into a silver box and drop it into the eye.
A plaster for flux of the eyes and other fluxes. Pound and sift mastic, frankincense, dry ladanum, aloe, and sorrel, take it up with egg whites, and use.

A fomentation for flux of the eye. Boil myrtle, tanner’s sumac, rose leaves, oak-galls, poppy-heads, split alum, and bramble root with vinegar, and foment the eyes with the decoction using a sponge. Vinegar-and-water warmed and applied likewise with a sponge is also effective. Or boil melilot, fenugreek, roses, date flesh, and poppy-heads with must or rainwater, and foment with a sponge.
For white spots on the eye. Burn bread, grind it with ammoniac salt and liver-colored aloe, and use, for it clears them away.
An eye-salve for the same. One ounce each of ammoniac salt, liver-colored aloe, cinnamon, and cinnamon bark; enough rose oil.

For old white spots. One pound of small oak-galls, one and a half ounces of blue vitriol, six ounces of myrrh; mix and grind, add Attic or Cretan honey, grind together well, store it, and anoint as needed.

For white spots and ulcers. Take clean sheep marrow from the thighs, free of bone, and pound it vigorously in a mortar, mixing in six ounces of oak-galls and some goose fat. Then grind it together, store it, and use it on deep ulcers, and you will fill them in.
An eye-remedy. Wash the root of centaury and boil it in water until it becomes soft, and press it out … when it is halfway done, add saffron, myrrh, Syrian nard—

By the same author, on determining the sex of the offspring. Thus will the sexes be distinguished according to nature. But it will also be produced artificially: a male, if you smear the horse’s member with hare’s blood and rennet (that is, the rennet of a newborn hare); a female, if for three days running you smear the mare’s vulva with goose fat together with turpentine resin, and then present her to the horse for mating.
If a mare cannot conceive. Write on her two flanks the forty-seventh psalm, as far as: ‘there pains as of a woman in labor.’

On the conception of a very barren mare — most necessary, for I write from much experience. Put three ounces of the blood of the sea-purple [murex shellfish], one ounce of niter, and two pounds of turpentine resin into the mare’s vulva. For once purified by this, she who was barren will become a mother.

For a barren mare to conceive. A bundle of leeks, and so on; or take … and put it into the mare’s vulva. For once purified by this, she who was barren will become a mother. Or write on a strip of paper and bind it on: ‘The gates of heaven opened of themselves, which the Hours kept.’

Aphrodisiacs to stimulate horses to mate. Saffron drunk with sweet wine, not much, is effective; or scammony rubbed on with water; or ground costus root drunk with mead; or the juice of mint; or a cock’s right testicle, salted, bound in a ram’s skin, and hung on the horse’s neck, is effective; or a stag’s dried testicle, scraped, and given to drink with honey-water.
For abundant milk. Soak barley in water; give the barley itself to eat, and give the water to drink, and it increases the milk.

By Africanus, on the generation of horses. If you wish a male to be born, turn the horses to face the east, so that while mating they look at the sun; for facing west produces females, as Maurusius the horse-breeder related. And indeed, as everyone says, it is believed that stallions are yoked to the Sun and are led by his flame, while mares, they say, are led by Night. And rightly so: the Sun is the maker of males, while the Moon, being of like nature, is mother of females.

By the same author, restoratives of strength. Myrrhis is a plant altogether resembling hemlock, except in its flower, which is likewise similar but much smaller; it has an elongated root, very fragrant and most pleasant to eat. It is found in cultivated land. Grind this whole plant carefully and put it into clean, well-boiled barley-gruel, and boil it together carefully, stirring. Then add as much very fragrant wine as will not make the gruel too liquid, and drench the fasting animal with it —

no better remedy for this could be found. If the root is unavailable, boiling pig marrow, especially spinal marrow, together with the gruel, and adding wine likewise, gives a second-best remedy for the same purpose.
From Aristotle, on mating. A horse begins to mate, and is mated, at two years old, so that it can even beget. However, the offspring—

—produced at this age are smaller and weaker. But for the most part it mates and is mated at three years old. It goes on producing ever better offspring up to twenty years of age. The male horse mates up to thirty-three years of age, and the mare is mated up to forty years, so that mating occurs almost throughout its life.
A horse for the most part lives about thirty-five years if male, the female more, up to forty. And indeed a horse has been known to live seventy-five years.
On the conception of a mare, by Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Hippocrates, greetings. I want you to know this too: if a mare does not retain the seed cast into her by the male but urinates it out, anoint your hand with oil, and, having pared your nails, insert it through her genitals and touch the womb.

And, sponging it with oil and wool, make a pessary of genuine purple-dye [murex], soak it in balsam-sap or henna oil, and place it in the womb, and immediately let the mare be covered by the stallion.
And after the horse has come down, do not let the mare stand still, but urge her to run. For in this way the seed cast into her will be retained more surely.

If the passage of the womb is closed from cold, foment it with old wine and work the place open with the finger, and having opened it, insert a pessary made of unwashed wool, pouring on it salt and raw niter.
Then immediately let the stallion be brought to the mare, and before the horse withdraws, remove the pessary and let him mount again, and—

—she will conceive. But if the passage has scarred over from a wound or another blow or a plague-related affliction, or has become doubled, cut it open and restore it to its natural state, or wipe it with sea-purple [murex].

Then, having ground frankincense, myrrh, saffron, and niter with rose oil and honey, pour it in for two days, having first fomented with a warm mixture and rubbed with oil, and after twenty days flush the womb with three ounces of milk. Do this for thirty days, and the mare will conceive, even if she was barren.
A stimulant, so that a horse will mount the mare many times.

Burn a stag’s tail, and so on; or one ounce of very old oil, six ounces of spurge-caterpillar. Gather these in summer, when the plant is in bloom, put them into the oil, and let it stand seven days. When needed, rub the loins and testicles with this oil. Pine caterpillars do the same. Or grind the fruit of the male mandrake, mix with honey and wine, and give as a drench. Wearing the fruit of eryngo also helps. Or half a hexagion of rocket seed, six carats of pepper,

ground with wine, and give as a drench. Or eighteen carats of ripe dill seed, ground with wine, and give as a drench. Or half a hexagion each of skink’s tail, ginger, cress seed, rocket seed, and pellitory, eighteen carats each of pepper and clove. The full dose is two hexagia six carats; for others, half a hexagion; the lesser dose eighteen carats.
A pessary to promote conception. One ounce of saffron, stag marrow,
goose fat, hare rennet, propolis, lily oil—
—prepare in equal parts and use. Or castoreum, hyssop, honey, butter, one ounce each of pig fat, enough oil of henna.
By Africanus, for much and effortless mating. Drench the animal with skink’s flesh in fragrant mixed wine.

A most excellent remedy for easy birth. Knotgrass is a common plant found everywhere, also called ‘drōsa.’ Bound into the afterbirth of a myrrh-treated and properly cleaned bitch, and worn as an amulet, it causes conception. And so that the animal may conceive whichever sex you wish, male or female: mercury and pellitory-of-Spain are held to be male and female according to their form — the upright ones male, the spreading ones female. Have the mare wear these together with the previous remedies: male ones if you wish a male born, female ones if a female.

By the same author, for abundance of milk. The stone called ‘galactites,’ worn tied to the animal’s udders, draws down a great quantity of milk. And so that she may have even more milk, give the galactites stone itself, ground, as a drench with wine and water.

By the same author, to prevent miscarriage of the embryo. Sailors take the remora fish and preserve it, using it as a most potent remedy both to prevent miscarriage and to aid conception. When ground and given as a drench, it keeps the animal’s unborn young safe within the belly. And if one brings a live one near the mare’s belly while the stallion is covering her, she will conceive then and ever afterward, and will never suffer the aforesaid mishap.
—incision. Use it thus, until it becomes clean.

Or soak a sponge in hot vinegar and bind it on for a day. Do this a second or third time. Then take the root of wild cucumber, chop it, sift it, and mix it in equal parts with barley meal, and, boiling it in water or hydromel, apply as a poultice. When it comes to suppuration, cauterize it with a straight cautery; having cauterized, anoint with fine salt and oil pounded together until it becomes like an ointment. Do this for six or eight days, until the scabs fall off. Then cleanse the wounds with urine and niter, foment with warm water and sponge them down, and treat with a wound-remedy and vetch-meal, until it is healed.
A resolvent for abscesses and scrofulous swellings. Grind white dog dung, mix with turpentine, and use.

A resolvent plaster that disperses abscesses. Mix half an ounce each of wax, oil, seawater, rosin, resin, and niter, and use. Or two ounces of fig-tree ash, one ounce each of split alum and soda-foam, seven ounces of liquid pitch, and use.

A dispersing and breaking-open plaster made with linseed juice. One ounce of old oil, twenty ounces of wax, half an ounce each of rosin and pig fat, one pound of litharge, six ounces of white lead, six ounces of linseed juice, one ounce of pollen, four ounces of frankincense; melt the meltable ingredients and add them to the dry ones, and use.
For scrofulous swellings. Boil cress seed and bean meal together, then add a little myrrh-oil, spread it on a cabbage leaf, and apply. Or take the root of balm-mint, gathered—
—while the moon is waning and in a barren sign, and apply it.
This makes scrofulous swellings and every bodily protrusion disappear
when worn as an amulet. And the stone called leontachates [lion-agate], and
the skin of a lion, worn as amulets, cure scrofula and all
bodily swellings. And the root of cyclamen, worn as an amulet,
and the root of mullein, taken in the name of the
sufferer and worn as an amulet, and the root of the single-stemmed houseleek, taken whole and
worn as an amulet, likewise cures.
By Ambrosius the sophist. Two ounces of shelled
Pontic nuts, six ounces of Gallic soap, five ounces of soda-foam,
six ounces each of the first runnings of soap and honey, the whites of six eggs, fourteen ounces of old oil, ten ounces of yellow wax, seven ounces of turpentine, four ounces
of chalcitis; prepare and use. Others outline the place with the sting of a sea-stingray and repeatedly touch its surface,
and it helps.
For pain of the jaw. If the jaw is in pain,
foment the horse with vinegar and pour on warm liquid, and
anoint with pig fat. And if it does not respond, cauterize with hot irons
and it will be healed.
For worms in the ears. Flush with a decoction
of wormwood or centaury or leek; drop in the juice of fresh caper
leaves or of the green fruit, or cedar-resin or old human urine, or white hellebore with honey, or the juice of calamint,
or scammony with vinegar, or the juice of wormwood. Oil dropped in
makes them float up to the top; better
—still is oil-and-vinegar. Use the same remedies also for small creatures that fall into the ears.

For discharging ears. Soak unripe oak-galls in the urine of an uncorrupted child, store it, and drop it in warm; or a decoction of pomegranate rinds with wine, or boil the juice of olive leaves with honey and use.

By Africanus, for earache. I wish to help the ears in a twofold way: so that the pain may cease, and, once ceased, not return. For when the affliction around the ear becomes hard to bear and foul-smelling, as sores form producing foul-smelling pus and breeding worms, and the pain around them becomes unbearable — the herb pellitory, common and growing everywhere, as though nature took pride in its abundance, is pounded vigorously so that much of its juice is extracted. Then a little Attic honey is added, not much sharp vinegar, and a small amount of sea-matter.
These, mixed and warmed, bring relief to the suffering ear.

For an ulcer. Put into the rind of a sweet pomegranate bull’s gall, oil, and honey in due proportion, and boil it in warm ash, then warm it and drop it in; or warm bull’s gall with woman’s milk and drop it in.
A remedy marvelous for pains and pus. Combine good fish-sauce and good honey and boil them in a pot to the consistency of honey, and drop it in; or burn and grind copper ore and blow it into the ear.
An ointment for the tonsils, tested by experience. Burn murex shells and claws, grind them together with honey, and anoint.
For boils. Before they come to a head, and so on; or dried figs—
—boiled figs mixed with resin, and apply.
On quinsy.

On quinsy, by Apsyrtus. Apsyrtus, and so on. As for the tongue, and so on; or pig dung, and so on. For quinsy sufferers the best treatment is by cautery. Failing that: five pounds of linseed, one and a half pounds of fenugreek, one pound eight ounces of vinegar, enough soft bread-crumbs; boil all together, knead with honey, and spread it on linen for a bandage, laying a clean sponge on top and binding it securely so that it does not fall off. One should also bleed this animal, opening the veins in the neck. This disease occurs in horses from being driven too hard.
A tested remedy for quinsy. Smear on dry white dog dung ground together with honey. This works wonderfully in humans too. Or smear on the ash of wild swallows kneaded with honey.
On nasal polyps, on ozaena, and on corns.

Another way. If a horse is troubled by nasal polyps, you will know it if it begins to discharge blood from the nostrils; treat it thus: six ounces each of frankincense, niter, and rue; drench through the nostrils with twenty ounces of dry wine, as much as needed, until it recovers. Or grind equal parts of black hellebore and realgar with oil, take it up in wool, and pack the nostril.

A remedy of Apollonius, natural philosopher. Slaughter a night-heron and smear the polyp with its warm blood while still hot. Dry the rest of the blood in the sun and sprinkle it on, quite dry. White dog dung ground with vinegar and smeared on also works excellently. Or grind equal parts of iron scale, copper scale, and split alum, and blow it in.

Tiberius’s remedy for horses affected at the coronet. Chop leeks and apply with salt and oil, and you will heal it the same day; or chop leeks and lard and apply; or grind the verdigris scraped from coins with vinegar and smear it all around the horse’s feet, the ozaenae and the cracks, and it heals at once.

A marvelous remedy for ozaenae. Soak coarse bread in vinegar for three days, and the next day grind male-leek leaves together and apply as a poultice with a cloth, having first washed with vinegar-and-oil. Or pound and sift split and round alum, copper ore, Egyptian thorn, and small oak-galls, mix with vinegar, and apply as a plaster, until they dry.
By Africanus, for ozaenae and polyps (on coughing). Grind the root of the winter-cherry with an equal part of butter, and use.
On coughing.

Tiberius’s remedy for the same. Lard, and so on. If a horse or other draught animal is troubled by cough, take old lard pounded together with edible pomegranate and put it into a woven basket, and, dipping it generously in honey, push the lump into the gullet. Let the basket have a firm handle about two cubits long, so that, drawing it back and forth, you can pull it out by the handle and lower it again. By this action and manipulation it is possible to set the animal right, whether the trouble in the gullet is a wound or a bone.
For cough. Give hulled, winnowed and ground lentils with three pounds of water, until it recovers.
A drench. Pig’s feet, and so on; or fenugreek juice,

half a hexagion of marjoram, three pounds of goat fat, thirty black figs, thirty dates, thirteen and a half ounces of honey. Or drench with wild cumin, wine, oil, and rue; or nine pounds of honey, and so on.

Another way. Slaughter a hen and immediately cut it open; take its belly just as it is, with its dung, and, rolling it in honey, give it to the animal still warm, through the mouth. Or mix one and a half ounces of barley-gruel and five ounces of must, and drench through the mouth. Also fumigate it with a compound like this: garlic heads, an equal amount of onions, two hexagia six carats of realgar, an equal amount of asphalt; grind these together, divide into three portions, and fumigate with one portion each time. Green fig-wood, or pine-wood, or cypress-wood, smoked—
—under the nostrils, also works.

After the fumigation, mix kid’s or sheep’s fat with sweet, pleasant wine, add wax, melt it, and pour it in through the mouth. Or warm ten ounces of old wine and one and a half ounces of oil, and drench for three days. Or grind tender rue leaves and pour them in through the nostrils with old wine, and sprinkle the fodder it eats with the juice of wild cucumber. Better still is the seed of the wild cucumber itself
and to mix the dried roots with barley and feed it this way. Or burn elm-wood, take the ash, and, straining it
into water together with an equal amount of oil and three eggs, give it.
Another natural remedy, well tested. Whole, unbruised wild sorrel

and so on; combine tragacanth, butter, iris, pig lard, split orpiment, and hyssop, and use. Or put squill into dough and bake it in the oven until the dough is toasted, then grind the squill, mix with good honey, and give it to the animal. Or give the flower of the reed-mace, and so on. This is beneficial for humans too.

Another remedy, good for humans too. Burn a clean white sponge to ash, combine it with an equal amount of pepper, grind with three and a half ounces of honey, and give half a hexagion in the evening, likewise in the morning. Or bind raven’s dung in unwashed wool and hang it on the neck, and it will stop. Or grind nine ounces of dried bay-berries and one ounce of myrrh from the Troglodyte country carefully, take it up with clarified honey, and give three hexagia at dawn and likewise in the evening: this has been tested. One ounce each of iris and hyssop, one and a half ounces of licorice, reduced by a third in water, then boiled together with enough honey,
drench a little for three days: this has been tested.

For chronic cough. One ounce each of anise seed, ammi seed, fennel seed, henbane, and pennyroyal; two ounces of tragacanth; one ounce of myrrh; grind it all, soak the tragacanth in ewe’s milk, mix, form into lozenges, and give half a hexagion each with warm mixed wine.

A linctus for those bringing up pus from coughing. Four and a half hexagia of storax reed, one ounce eighteen carats of male frankincense, one and a half ounces each of turpentine, hyssop, and iris, three ounces of vetch-meal, two pounds three ounces of skimmed honey. The dose is half a hexagion.
On distortion of the neck.
On fever.
If it feels pain in the shoulder-joint, and so on; or soda, and so on. For pain of the shoulders, bleed the animal, then boil frankincense-manna together with wine over the shoulders,
and anoint.
For putrefaction.

—cannot void. It urinates black and thick urine. Some of them also have difficulty urinating frequently, and crouch down, and arch the loins, and become bent, and their bodies collapse, and they urinate blood. For pain occurs about the kidneys and the bladder. Indeed the organs press upon one another because of their continuity, and the fluids burst forth before being excreted from the belly into the kidney. Then they collect likewise in the bladder, and pains and separations occur similarly in the kidneys. For the most part, then, we find that inflammation produces either blockage or ulceration.
This comes from certain fluids possessing an acrid quality.

It is treated thus: foment the hips and loins with boiled vetch, adding celery seed or anise or one of the other diuretics. Foment, having first anointed the hips with wax-salve. Use diuretic food too — fennel, celery, barley, radishes, and anise — and give green alfalfa if you have it; if not, sprinkle it with must. Give white chickpeas too, soaked in wine for about an hour.

For drink use wheat flour, or in summer barley flour, about a pound a day dissolved in barley-gruel, and let it stand in an open space. Also drench it with a pound of figs poured into three pounds four ounces of water, boiled down to half and strained, and grind together three ounces of celery seed, three ounces of wild carrot, eight parts of anise, four and a half hexagia of myrrh; grind these with ten ounces of sweet wine and pour it in through the mouth.

and use gentle walks. If it does not respond, do this as well, and give it an enema: peel the bark from mullein root and boil it with wine. Then grind it as fine as possible, strain it, mix it with warm water, and use this as an enema. Let the whole enema be about three pounds four ounces. And spread as much straw bedding under it as possible.

Do this until you see the urine clear, the testicles firm, and the feet stepping forward not less than six finger-widths. For the enema foments the kidneys from within and makes the region light, while what is given through fodder, diuretics, and drenches expels quickly and thinly the corruption flowing to the bladder and kidneys, along with the flow of blood, so that no disease results. But if, after doing this, it does not recover, cauterize it around the last rib and the flank, measuring three finger-widths from the spine. For in this way the humors will fall away outward.
After cauterizing, treat the sores as described above.

For dislocation of the hip, if the tendon is severed. If the hip-joint of a horse or other draught animal is dislocated, do not treat it: for the connecting tendon does not lie in the socket, but tears near the bone called the ‘hollow’ bone, because of its depth. For when the so-called condyle rolls and slips out forcibly, the tendon cannot hold it — especially when it is stretched more than it should be — but it tears when this happens.
—so if you force it back into place, it will spring out again, because the bone does not hold the tendon.
For this reason, then, it cannot be treated.
A kidney antidote of the Patriarch Theophylact.
One hexagion of true cinnamon, three hexagia each of asarum, clove, spikenard, and long, white, and common pepper; grind and reduce by a third with fresh water, and drench with old wine.
A tested remedy for sciatica.
Burn dry cabbage stalks and take up the ash with old fat, and apply as a poultice.
On pain of the belly.
Another way for pain of the belly. If a draught animal, horse, or any other creature has pain in its belly, these signs will follow: it falls and groans suddenly, and contracts, and cannot stand.

Take cabbage leaves, chop and strain them, and mix with ten ounces of sweet wine and nine ounces of oil, and, having ground it, pour it in through the nostrils; or grind birthwort root and germander with wine and pour it in through the mouth.
Or likewise grind onion leaves with ten ounces of wine and pour it in.
By Eumelus, on flux of the belly.
Draw blood from the veins in the head, and so on; or dissolve one and a half ounces of cucumber in honey and give as an enema.
On tilix.

If a horse is troubled by tilix (that is, if it ‘tzila’s’), examine its belly: for it will be swollen and hard. Then draw blood from the forelegs, and let it abstain from barley until the belly settles, and drench it three times with horehound and wormwood.
Foment it with hot water.
If it does not stop, treat the—

—of worms, that is: ‘saw-worms,’ common worms, and pinworms (some have called these long, flat, and round). It is not our purpose here to speak of names, but of remedies. The animal twisted up by these is treated as described variously above.

Another way, on strangury. There are signs of this affliction, though not the same in all. Some thrust out their genitals and shake themselves, wanting to urinate; others dribble from the genitals and are drawn up, and, putting their nostrils to their flanks, sniff at them. Others crouch down on their haunches, others lash themselves under the thighs with their tails, others bite at what is nearby and paw the ground with their hind feet. This affliction is dangerous. If, then, you notice any such sign, anoint

your hand and insert it into the rectum up to the elbow. If the bladder, being distended, meets your hand, rub it gently, and if it still does not urinate, boil two ounces two hexagia of celery seed with ten ounces of wine and nine ounces of oil, and drench. Let it walk about, and encourage it to urinate. Or mix one ounce of opopanax with vinegar and drench; or grind chaste-tree fruit with wine and oil, boil, and drench. Or crush lumps of salt or an onion and insert them into the rectum, and it will urinate.
Another way. A horse suffering from strangury should be fed on green fodder; mix in as many celery leaves as possible. If it will not eat the celery, grind it and give it with

warm water, and it will recover. Above all, foment with warmth the area under the belly, the testicles, and the anus, and then the rest of the body. If it persists, warm two and a half pounds of wine and an equal amount of water, add finely ground soda-foam, and administer as an enema with a bladder-syringe.

For those unable to urinate. On the animal’s left hoof, with your left hand, write — better with a bronze stylus, or failing that even an iron one — the name of its own master, and say into its left ear three times: ‘The cock does not urinate water.’ It has been tested.

By Africanus, on difficult urination. If a horse’s urine is retained, let a virgin loose her girdle and strike it across the face with the girdle, and it will urinate copiously at once, and the pain will cease.

By Theomnestus, on the same. The disease of difficult urination is threefold. When one urinates with difficulty, it is called ‘dysuria’; when in dribbles, ‘strangury’; when it does not urinate at all, ‘ischuria,’ which, if not treated, quickly proves fatal. [When it comes slowly, that is strangury.] Many technical remedies have been written by the ancients for ischuria — treatment with garlic and onions, and the eversion of the bladder through the anus — which are remedies more dangerous than the disease itself rather than safe. I will set out what we ourselves have often applied with success. First one must know that all forms of difficult urination arise from cold, or from being driven too hard, or from blockage. It is fitting to heat
water in a cauldron and, having first anointed with oil using sponges,
pour the warm water tolerably from the kidneys down to the tail.
Stand the horse in a warm room free of draughts, and, relaxing, it will urinate.
Also drench through the nostrils and the mouth with five ounces of sweet wine, and it will urinate.

If that is not at hand, boil asparagus seed or the asparagus stalks themselves, and drench through the nostrils and mouth with their water mixed with sweet wine and oil; or drench with as much opopanax as a grape, dissolved in wine-and-oil — this is for very large cases.
For difficult urination in a mare. Say into her right ear three times: ‘The horse calls you — do not withhold your water.’
A marvelous diuretic drench. Dry the flesh of the land hedgehog in the sun, grind it, and give it with wine through the mouth; likewise the preserved and dried contents of its belly do the same.
Or take two or three of the wood-lice found under water-jars, boil them with a little fish-sauce, mix in a little water, and drench. It works excellently.
By Tiberius. If the bladder is blocked, mix fennel juice and anise with water and sweetened wine, warm it, and pour it into the rectum.
Or fumigate the horse, covered with blankets, with the preserved and dried entrails of the land hedgehog.
Or warm one and a half ounces each of leek juice and wine and drench; or reduce one bunch of dill by a third in wine and drench.
For a horse suffering from strangury. Four and a half hexagia of rhubarb, one ounce of valerian,
four hexagia of lovage, four hexagia each of asarum and parsley, nine carats of Celtic nard; pound and give with spiced wine. Or give eighteen carats of ring-dove dung with honey as a drench.

Another natural remedy. Fumigate with stag’s hair. Wearing a bat also helps the animal. Burn decayed human teeth, grind them, and give them with fat mixed into food to the ailing animal: it helps excellently.
On tetanus and opisthotonos.
On diarrhea.
Another way: prognosis and cure. For a horse suffering from diarrhea, and so on; or silphium juice, and so on; or boil beets with must and drench with cucumber-and-niter water.
An enema for diarrhea. Mix black wine with an equal amount of water, add a little oak-gall, and if it does not stop, give it dog dung to drink with dry white wine.

Or heat iron red-hot and quench it in wine, add ground cumin, and give to drink. Or dry and grind hens’ gizzards and sprinkle them into the drink; or grind oak acorns with wine and give. Or take sea-crabs or river-crabs, burn the shells, and give with water; or burn earthworms on potsherds to ash and drench with dry wine, and, having roasted and chopped bay leaves, burnt pennyroyal and oak-galls, grind all in equal parts, and drench with wine.
On remedies for twisted gut and for wind.
A powder for a prolapsed rectum, tested by experience. Burnt haircloth, burnt wool-felt, and—
—also burnt, and dry pitch, both in equal parts; make a powder and sprinkle it on the protruding rectum, having first anointed it with pitch-oil, and push it back until it goes in, and it will heal.
On volvulus.
A fomentation for the same. Boil together rue, cumin, fleabane, dill, and cardamom in oil, and, soaking wool in it, apply it as hot as possible.
A drench. Boil dill in oil and water and drench. Pure balsam given as a drench also helps them marvelously.
On effusion, on dropsy, and on tympanites.

For tympanites — this also works on humans. Combine and grind celery seed, fennel seed, cumin, anise, galingale, bay-berries, fenugreek, linseed, darnel from wheat, goat dung, vinegar, and honey, and use.
By Africanus, for dropsy. Drench with crow fat in twenty ounces of warm wine; or burn a land hedgehog and drench with its ash in wine.

A dropsy plaster, the barber’s. Four pounds of dry pitch, two pounds of wax, one pound of pine-resin, eight ounces each of fenugreek meal, black chamaeleon-thistle root, and pollen, four ounces of ground cumin; prepare and use.

Another, which absorbs the surrounding fluid. One ounce each of very finely ground dry cabbage roots and washed lime, three ounces of squirting-cucumber juice, three pounds of old fat; make into a soft plaster and, spreading it on linen, apply.
The ‘caulker’s’ soft plaster for dropsy and swelling of the spleen, which reduces the swelling. Roasted pine-resin—

—four pounds, wax and pitch two pounds each, liquid alum, red niter, birthwort, ammoniac incense, cardamom-scented bdellium, prepared mistletoe-gum, myrrh, wild cucumber root, and sycamore-fig sap, three ounces each, three pounds of old oil, two and a half pounds of vinegar.
On dysentery.
By Apsyrtus. Apsyrtus to Chaireas, and so on; or grind the liver of the kite called ‘loupous’ with milk and give as a drink.

Another way. These are the signs of dysentery: the belly becomes distended with wind, foul odors occur, and it passes matter that is mucous, windy, and chilled. Wash the belly, then, with warm water, and give as fodder alfalfa mixed with milk, about two and a half pounds. Lemnian earth, too, drunk with wine, cures dysentery sufferers, after the gut has first been flushed with honey-water. Or make very fine pumice with wine and eggs and drench; or chop dry fig leaves and drench with dry wine. Or chop equal parts of macer bark and pomegranate rind and drench with wine. Or boil the shells of Pontic hazelnuts

in wine and drench with a little aloe; or boil bramble roots with dark wine and drench with their decoction, for it helps colic and dysentery sufferers. Or take up oak-galls, heath fruit, and opium, half an ounce each, in water, and drench with pomegranate wine.

The Berytian lozenge for dysentery. One and a half hexagia each of spikenard, saffron, and myrrh, the juice of hypocist, liver-colored aloe, Theban opium, unripe oak-gall, anise, and acacia gum; pound and sift, take up with wine, and make into loz—
—enges, and use, washing them down with wine.
On the spleen.

Another way. From the shoulders, and so on; or drench through the nostrils with three hexagia eighteen carats of chaste-tree seed with vinegar-and-water; or give eighteen carats each of roasted squill and caper-root bark likewise with vinegar-and-water; or grind and sift equal parts of hedysarum seed (that is, sainfoin), hart’s-tongue fern, sharp-dock root, costus, anise, and spleenwort, and drench through the left nostril.

A soft plaster for the spleen. Two ounces each of fatty bdellium, calf fat, ammoniac incense, and iris; six hexagia each of opopanax, galbanum, spelt grain, and storax; one hundred sixty grains of pepper, six ounces of wax, two and a half ounces of iris oil, enough wine. Pound and sift the dry ingredients; melt the meltable ones and add them to the dry; dissolve the ammoniac, opopanax, frankincense, and bdellium in the wine, and, having softened it, use. For it is of the utmost softening power — you could not find anything more softening than it. Amythaon’s soft plaster and Asclepion’s also help.

Another natural soft plaster. Pound and sift cyclamen — if fresh is available, grind it — and take it up with pounded fatty dried figs, sprinkling a little vinegar on the figs an hour beforehand. Then combine, spread on a cloth, and apply. On the first day the spleen will soften, on the second it will be healed, and on the third, if you anoint it, it will be reduced still further. The soft plaster made with bay-berries also helps.
On wood-worms.
Tiberius’s remedy for wood-worms and intestinal worms. Take

dried mucus, dried figs, wormwood, fenugreek, and dried lupines, and boil them down until they form a broth. Then put into the broth two ounces two hexagia of cress and a little honey, and drench for seven days, keeping the animal off barley. After the drench, walk it about, feed it, and give it drink, and you will heal it.
On blood discharged through the rectum.

Another way. Leek juice, and so on. But if it brings up blood through the nostrils, and so on; for those vomiting blood, and so on. For those bleeding from the nostrils, drench with comfrey root and tragacanth soaked in wine.
A poultice for the same. Apply to the hips a raw dissolution kneaded with vinegar-and-water or rose oil.
For those vomiting blood. Drench with eighteen carats of hematite stone with pomegranate juice, or likewise with coral stone.
Or drench through the mouth with equal parts of split earth, ageratum stone, and Lemnian earth, with plantain juice.
On haemouria and haemorrhage and styptics, and
that haemouria arises from weakness of the kidneys and dryness
of the lung. Apsyrtus to Artemas of Carthage,
greetings. Having heard that you are greatly distressed with grief
over the affliction that has befallen your horse, I do not hide
the truth from you, since the evidence lies in experience,
for nothing among these matters is hidden. It is difficult, then, that by undertaking treatment
we shall succeed in curing it. For haemouria is
rather a discouraging condition. For this reason one must hold back and act only after careful
consideration and caution, so that we may undertake the treatment with due care.

Let us then apply to it all warming and relaxing remedies, fomenting the loins with sponges; then, boiling elm root, fleabane, tree-mallow, and mountain pennyroyal until reduced by a third, let us pour it on in this way; then, wiping away the horse’s sweat, let us rub it down with wine-and-oil and butter, and use these unusual drenches: roast the bird called the crested lark in a pot, feathers and all, and grind it with honey-wine,
adding to the broth pepper and leaf [malabathrum] and unripe-olive oil

and give it through the mouth for three days, and then, changing the remedy, drench with butter and roasted cumin together with parsley and old wine. And let the rubbing-down with wine-and-oil be done more frequently.
The lark treatment is suited to human kidney patients too.
Haemouria arises from over-exertion, and often also from cold. We have also given cucumber-and-niter with must, and it did no harm. Give also

the remedy made with unripe-olive oil and honey for three days, on account of the roasting effect on inflammations; and, alternating, boil a pig’s trotter, adding trefoil and honey-wine, and drench with the broth; or boil barley-water, and a puppy — if a puppy is not available, give lard — for three days.
How to check a heavy flow of blood coming down from the palate. When you have bled the horse, and so on; or take old harness-leather
burn it, sift it, and blow it in with a reed, and you will stop it. Or two ounces of sponge, one ounce each of burnt lead and antimony; make a powder and use.
A styptic remedy of Oribasius, effective also against spreading sores in the genitals and scrotum. Honey and rose oil kneaded together, unfired sulphur, orpiment, realgar, and lime, in equal parts.
Another excellent remedy for haemorrhage. Take up gypsum with pollen and egg white, mix in goat hair, and apply.
Another powerful remedy. Four hexagia each of split alum, blue vitriol, and oak-gall, one ounce of copper ore, half an ounce of iron scale.
On blockage.

Another way. If a horse or other draught animal is troubled by a blockage, it does not easily survive. These are the accompanying signs: it rolls about and paws the ground, and strains as though wanting to urinate, its armpits sweat, sometimes the whole body too, tremors occur, and it turns toward its belly; yet it does pass some dung, and some urine is discharged. This disease occurs for the most part when some obstruction becomes lodged in the passages of the rectum. For it becomes distended with wind and, growing over-strained, dies.

It is treated thus: anoint your hand and insert it into the rectum, and draw out what is lodged there, and, having poured in about four ounces of oil, make it walk about as gently as possible. Foment its belly, the area around the navel, and the chest. Whenever you are not fomenting it, keep it gently moving by walking it about—

—and give it an enema thus: soak bran in warm water for about an hour, strain off about six to eight ounces, mix in eighteen ounces of niter and four and a half ounces of honey, and give as an enema. Or grind opopanax and celery seed in ten ounces of white wine and pour it in through the nostrils. Or grind opopanax, wild-carrot seed, three bay-berries, and niter, and, adding eight and a half ounces of fragrant wine and four and a half hexagia of myrrh and half an ounce of Ethiopian cumin, grind with old wine and honey and pour it in likewise.

If it does not respond to these treatments, take a large clyster-syringe and inject warm water through the mouth as forcefully as possible. Then, raising it up, keep it gently moving by walking. The next day give it about three ounces of wheat flour in warm water to drink. Feed it, if it will take it, soft leavened bread, and offer nothing else, since otherwise the belly becomes constricted and it is in danger.
On strophos.

An enema. Boil beets, and so on; or write [a charm], and so on; or strike the horse with colic lightly with a storax-wood rod; or slaughter a chick and, taking its belly with its entrails still warm, hold the horse’s tongue and throw it into its mouth. Or boil marjoram in wine and give it to drink, or use Philo’s remedy.
On empty straining.
On rupture of the chest.
On prolapse of the penis.
For cracks in the penis. Roasted pine resin, ground with rose oil until it has the consistency
of honey, boiled saffron, and applied — greatly helps; or burnt dry ivy leaves ground with oil in a leaden mortar, and applied to the cracks.
On inflammation of the testicles.

Another way. Chalky earth, and so on; or put hot millstone-fragments or potsherds into human urine, and fumigate the inflamed parts with the vapor; then pour the urine itself over the testicles; then apply a plaster of wine or vinegar with burnt hay, salt, and cumin mixed and ground together, and you will cure it.
If the scrotum swells, take the heaviest part of a balance-beam, burn it, combine it with fat, and apply twice a day: this is the best of all the above remedies; or smear the scrotum with goose gall.

Another way. Bring it into cold water, and smear with Cimolian earth mixed with honey-water; or grind linseed and fenugreek with honey-water and apply as a poultice; or knead fresh wine-lees with fine barley-meal and smear on; for a burning sensation, chop and combine lily root, fleabane, and green coriander with raisins, their pips removed, and smear on; or combine eighteen carats of balsam, one and a half ounces of niter, four and a half hexagia of dove dung, two and a half ounces of galbanum, and the same of turpentine, and use; or grind yellow onion bulbs with salt, make into a plaster, and apply — for it draws tight and relieves the swelling upward.
On intestinal hernia.
Another way. [lacuna] two ounces, frankincense, artificial glue, myrrh, aloe, three ounces each, eight ounces of tanner’s pomegranate rind, of balaustium [pomegranate flower]
On flux in the knees and feet.
On flux in the feet, that is, chilblains. Apsyrtus

to Apollonides, and so on; this too we know from experience: one ounce each of verdigris and honey — but if it discharges moisture, also two ounces of litharge — anointing the pasterns. We have also learned that seal fat works well.
If it has a swollen shin. Rub it down thoroughly with haircloth, until it even draws blood. Then apply vetch-meal with honey and let it be worn for three days.

For every kind of flux and inflammation, and for afflictions of the sinews, joints, and varicose veins. The horse with flux gnaws at its joints and stamps the ground with its feet. We ought therefore to check its flux thus: grind together white lead, litharge, zinc oxide, burnt copper, and vinegar-and-rose-oil or astringent wine, and smear the swollen cords. If the flux persists and produces sores, use this astringent compound: boil frankincense, mastic, rosin, pitch, pine-resin, bull’s or goat’s fat, and mastic-oil or myrtle-oil, and apply as a poultice. Use also an astringent fomentation: boil mastic, Sicilian myrtle, tender bramble-shoots, cypress-balls, and oak-galls with old wine, and foment.
Another remedy for flux caused by a varicose vein. We shall recognize that the flux comes from a varicose vein when a swelling forms around the knee. The swelling forms in this way:

when the vessel lying above, over the shoulder-blade, having collected, flows down to the upper foreleg and fills the knee, and, the lower vessel not accommodating the excess, it backs up and produces the swelling and causes lameness. This is called a varix. One must therefore cut the upper foreleg, as described above, to open the vessel. But if a swelling lies above, cut the skin with a scalpel, so that the pressure in the vessel may escape outward and be released, and it will quickly subside. Use also the rest of the treatment, and you will heal it.
Another cauterizing remedy for soft swellings and swellings in the joints. Pound squill and lard, mix in sharp vinegar, and apply as a plaster to the hoof for ten days, and it will be healthy.
For a flow of flux. Smear on rose oil, starch, and egg white.
For foreign, unclean matter in a wound. Knead dog dung with vinegar and apply as a poultice. It works marvelously.
A tested remedy for stiff joints. Six ounces each of wax, bull fat, and pine-resin, three ounces of greasy wool, two and a half ounces of old lard.

For fluxes and swellings — this helps humans too. Gather the bark of elm-root and boil it until soft. Then pound it until it becomes like dough, and, rolling it in barley flour, fry it, adding some of the elm-root broth, and when sufficiently cooked, spread it on a cloth, and, spreading butter over it, apply it to the swollen and flux-affected place.
For every inflammation. Chop wild cucumber and apply—
—and you will marvel.
For hard swelling. Boil marshmallow, fenugreek, linseed, and pollen, and apply.
Hierocles’s remedy for pain of the knees. Boil rue in oil and anoint.
For swelling from flux or a kick. Knead goose fat with sharp vinegar and bind it on, having first anointed the place because of the hair.
A poultice for swelling of the joints from a blow or any other cause. Knead asphalt and pollen with vinegar and apply as a poultice.

To harden the cartilage of an animal. Grind verdigris and the scale that falls from the anvil, and, making a powder, mix them in equal parts, and, having washed the cartilage with oil, sprinkle it on.

For swelling of the fetlocks. If the fetlocks swell from running or from flux, clear the place with a depilatory, prick it, and make many close punctures. Then take a warm ox lung, still warm, apply it, and bind it on, and leave it from the hour it was applied until the same hour the following day, then apply another lung likewise. Do this three or even four times, until you have healed it.
On marble-disease.
On gout.

By Apsyrtus. Apsyrtus to Artemas, and so on, and it recovers. Or grind celery seed, myrrh, and frankincense, four ounces each, dissolving the celery mostly in white wine, and pour it into the left nostril — not more than five ounces, but not less either — as much as seems sufficient, judging by the horse’s strength.
Another way. First one must cut the third wattle on the left side and let it—
—bleed, no less than half a pound nor more.
The next day cut the hind ones below the hocks and let an equal amount flow, and foment with fragrant wine, adding myrrh, frankincense-manna, and galbanum, and whatever else is fragrant.
Warm the pot over a charcoal fire of vine-cuttings, and foment from the neck upward, holding it underneath.

Wash the mouth with warm water, sponging down the rest of the body too, and especially the loins, having anointed them with warm oil; one should rub them and keep a fire burning nearby and cover it, until it sweats.

Then release the heat gradually, removing the coverings, so that it is not chilled suddenly, and give the drench on the third day, and feed it moist fodder, especially horehound or celery leaves, if it will eat them, mixing in lettuce too, and whatever else it likes, and washed couch-grass rinsed in warm water; force it to eat cress leaves, and give a warm drink, and about eighteen pounds of ground barley, giving the same care again in the evening.
Let it be exercised a little, according to its condition, as it is disposed, so that it does not secretly suffocate from the remedy and fall into a worse illness.
Another gout remedy, a marvel. Oil, wine, common salt: boil until the salt dissolves, and use.
On loss of hair and on shagginess.
If, in a sick animal, the hair stands on end.
Warm honey and milk, as much as the hand holds, and drench through the nostril.
On growing hair on animals. Grind soot from a kitchen or

bath-house fine in a mortar, and, adding sharp vinegar, smear it on — not all over the animal at once, so that it is not distressed by the sharpness, but on the part where the cause is greatest, say the thigh or the neck, and it will grow hair again within three days. If one is pressed for time on a journey, it is not necessary to grind the soot in a mortar, but, coarse as it is, smear it on with brine. For the soot is broken down by the sharpness of the vinegar just like chalk.

Another very powerful hair-growing remedy. Roast barley with beans, and burn goat horn and human hair and reed bulbs, grind them all, and take them up with bear fat. This also works on humans, even against baldness.

A transformation. Whenever a man tending the herd wishes a black or chestnut or dappled or white mare’s foal to come out gleaming with golden hair over white, let him, near the accustomed spring in the green pastures, set up an image blended from many-colored dyes, and, as the mare drinks and looks upon it with thirsty eyes, as though drawn by desire toward a union imagined in love, she will bring forth young resembling the horse she gazed upon. For whatever many-colored patterns her mind has drunk in through sight, the belly too will bring forth and give birth to a likeness of these.

By Africanus, on the color of horses. Horses differ, as in their virtues, so also in their colors. It is a piece of good fortune, and a mark of dignity for the animal, to have an even coat. Some colors are natural to them, while others—

—are artificially produced by some who change them for the better: some are altered with drugs, others are made mottled by branding. A chestnut horse could become black if plastered with squill ground with vinegar and pumice, and would come out white if the remedy is applied hot. A chestnut could be produced from white by grinding lime and litharge, boiling them in water to the consistency of a paste, and plastering it on for two hours; but if the application is left on for more hours, a white horse would come out black instead. Apart from actual dyes, fire too works upon the animal’s coat to give it a different appearance, and counterfeits dappling in the horse. A ‘white-dappled’ horse (this is the name for that coloring) is produced in this way: a round cauterizing iron, hollow in the middle, bent into the circumference of the letter omicron, is heated and applied, while the horse is restrained, by repeated touching and lifting. The ring itself comes out black on the outside, while the original coat remaining within it counterfeits a leopard’s spots, when arranged over the legs and neck. One might even see its face made to look like a wild beast’s. This is a fine thing to brand on a spirited horse, so that its speed may match its coat.

An excellent hair-dye. Soak black fig-tree leaves in rainwater, grind them vigorously, and, having first clipped the horse close, apply as a poultice. This treatment ensures once and for all that the hair never turns white again.
By Africanus, a hair-dye that lasts forever.

—six ounces each of maidenhair fern, two hexagia six carats of oak-gall, ten green walnuts, one and a half pounds of black myrtle from the blood, six ounces of ladanum, five ounces of old dark wine. Boil it all with wine until reduced by a third, and, having cleaned the hair, dip it in for three days and nights, and you will marvel.
On horses that pull out their hair.
On herpes and night-pustules.

Another way, on herpes. A bilious and acrid humor, striking down into some part of the body, produces herpes. And if bile happens to collect there, it produces the corroding herpes through its violent acridity, so that it not only passes through all the internal parts but even through the skin as far as the epidermis, which alone it corrodes and eats through, gradually taking hold of the continuous skin — hence it is called ‘herpes.’ And if the bile mixes also with phlegm, it produces the other kind of herpes, called ‘millet-herpes,’ which raises protrusions on the skin like millet grains.

The treatment is this: one must apply as a poultice ground vine-tendrils or bramble leaves, together with knotgrass and plantain. Later, mix in boiled lentils with these, and sometimes barley-meal and honey too.

An excellent remedy for herpes and all eruptions occurring on the surface. Burn goat horn, grind it with vinegar, and smear it on. Burn the horn thus: holding it over a fire, shake off the rising bubbles into a mortar, until it is all used up. Sheep horn works too, especially that of the ram. Its ash also works
taken up excellently in a liquid wax-salve; or half an ounce of split alum, one and a half hexagia of blue vitriol, and an equal amount of rock salt, taken up in vinegar, and used.
Another marvelous remedy. Take up equal parts of niter, chalcitis, blue vitriol, copper ore, lime, and acacia gum in vinegar, and use with water.

A wax-salve for skinned herpes-sores. One and a half hexagia each of white lead, litharge, alkanet root, and burnt oak-gall, eighteen carats of frankincense-manna, the same of split alum, two ounces of wax, twelve and a half ounces of calf fat, five ounces of oil, the whites of two eggs; grind the dry ingredients with wine and, having prepared it, apply.
On porcupine-quill-like eruptions.
On ulceration of the mouth and on aphthae of the tongue.
Tiberius’s remedy for those with flux in the mouth and drooling. Knead marjoram with salt and linseed with honey, and give it to chew.

For sores in the mouth. Grind oak-gall and red sumac in equal parts and rub the mouth with it; also pull the tongue out and rub it, and hold the whole mouth shut, so that it may be drawn tight. Do this twice a day until it is healed. Or grind two ounces two hexagia of cress, ground cabbage leaves, and ten ounces of wine to the consistency of honey and
drench likewise. Or grind wormwood leaves with ten ounces of wine and drench, or grind birthwort root with wine and drench.
On animals exhausted from a journey or a race, and on those with sores on the flanks.

Diagnosis of the ‘fivefold affliction’: chill, straining, exhaustion, rupture, trembling. Apsyrtus to the centurion Romulus, greetings. You informed me, my lord Romulus, that a combination of several afflictions has occurred, and that the animal has been seized by it.

I found myself in great perplexity and distress at the sudden and overwhelming combination of such an illness. From what, then, should we recognize the combination of the disease, and what are its component afflictions?
The afflictions are: trembling, chill, rupture, exhaustion, and straining. For this reason it is called the ‘fivefold affliction.’

We must establish the source of each of these. Trembling comes from weakness; chill comes from cold sweat dripping from cold and distress; exhaustion and straining come from the animal throwing itself to the ground, unable to bear the exhaustion, but overcome by the strain. Rupture comes from sleeplessness, from which sometimes the flanks are also drawn up, and wind is continually passed through the rectum.
