We shall show, then, how each of these afflictions ought to be checked. For the trembling: soak dry bread in water, then press out the water, flush it with fragrant wine, and give it, so that it may gain strength, and with the wine

sprinkle it over the whole body, and make the hand-rubbing firmer, and let it be gently exercised. For the chill, give oil of henna through the nostrils, and use warming, relaxing ointments; for the relief of the straining, pound garlic and old lard together with butter, cumin, and old wine, and rub it in from the loins to the spinal marrow, for it will benefit both.

For the filling, that is the rupture, of the gut, give warming and richly oily drenches, adding pellitory and cumin juice and barley for three days, and then, alternating for another three days, give a gruel of fine wheat flour boiled with marjoram. For the straining, soak greasy wool in warm water and lay it repeatedly on the loins, and drench with the very grease itself, and let its stall be warm and well-lit.

Feed it every kind of food gradually, if it happens to lose its appetite; if there is green fodder, so much the better; if not, sprinkle the dry fodder with honey-water and give it barley too. At the outset draw blood, both from the neck and from the temples, and drench with goat’s milk mixed with saffron. Apply the phlebotomy, as has been said, only at the start; once the disease has passed its peak, no longer — for once the strength has been reduced, death easily follows.
Treatment for one injured by running or other exhaustion. For one whose bones and sinews ache from toil and exhaustion, mix oil with water so that they blend,
and anoint the horse’s whole body against the grain of the hair, vigorously, until it recovers. For this is no less important than the rest.
On ulceration of the windpipe and throat.

On rupture of the windpipe and blockage of the throat, that is, a deposit of phlegm. If a horse or other draught animal suffers a ruptured windpipe, the affliction is serious. These are its signs: it breathes heavily and wheezes, and coughs, and snorts, and discharges purulent mucus, and its body wastes, and when it neighs its voice is thin, and the flank is drawn up and does not fill out with the body, but becomes fleshless. Some of them also go lame in the forelegs. Such animals die more slowly.

Draw blood, then, from the neck, and let three pounds flow, and, having stopped the flow, anoint it with wine and oil. Give a drench of two pounds of figs poured into ten pounds of water. Boil these until reduced by half, and drench through the mouth during the day; or soak three ounces of tragacanth in water overnight, and in the morning grind it, pour on twenty ounces of wine, and drench through the mouth.

On ulceration of the windpipe. In this case use bull’s gall continually. If the upper chest becomes painful and swells, boil barley meal with wine and apply it as a poultice to the place twice a day. When it becomes soft and forms an internal sore, treat it as described above under sores.
A windpipe remedy. Six ounces of tragacanth, one ounce of kermes-berry, enough pepper and honey. Soak the tragacanth beforehand.
On asthma.
A poultice for the same. Combine fatty figs, darnel meal, and barley meal with resin and wax, iris, and frankincense-manna, and apply as a plaster over the chest.
A drench for the same. Knead equal parts of germander, southernwood, castoreum, ground-pine, and ammoniac incense with honey, and drench with honey-water.
On those inflamed from travel.
Tiberius’s remedy for the same. Chop parsley, chia seed, wild carrot, celery, southernwood, and celery seed, and reed-mace flower, and take it up with old wine.

For animals overheated and slow to recover. Put a handful of dry wormwood into a vessel of wine the day before and soak it; the next day, having pressed out the wormwood, grind it in a mortar carefully until smooth. Then add two ounces of saffron, grind again, and enough honey, and, having stirred it, give it as a drink first. And make it exercise a great deal. Do this for up to three days. This is for one animal; if you wish to drench several, adjust it according to the animals and their constitutions.
On those burned by lye.

By Apsyrtus. If, and so on; also rub on copper flower in boiled vinegar to the consistency of honey, and use. Or grind pickled olives with barley-meal and apply as a poultice, or grind split alum with vinegar, or bull’s gall with water. Or pour lye mixed with fish-sauce over it and apply as a plaster, or lily bulbs with narcissus, adding rose oil, make it into an ointment and use. Or dip a rag in honey, roll it in barley, and burn—

and add three ounces of the ash, three hexagia of white lead, three hexagia of butter, two ounces each of wax, goat fat, and rose oil, and, having combined them, use. Or grind pine bark and dry maidenhair fern, and use. Or burn myrtle leaves, dissolve in vinegar, and smear on; or white lead with a little stag marrow is a good remedy.

On those burned by fire. Animals burned by fire or hot water should be smeared at once, so as to prevent inflammation, with whatever earth is at hand — with water for those of tender flesh, with vinegar-and-water for the rest, and best of all with Cimolian earth. For any light earth does the same, as does a whole raw egg taken up in soft wool and applied, and frankincense ground with water, and raw or boiled beet leaves applied as a poultice with wine, and any kind of alum with water and egg white.

For burns that have been skinned and ulcerated. Bind dove dung in a linen cloth and burn it, and grind the ash with wine and smear it on; or take it up in a wax-salve and use it — it is a tested remedy.

An excellent remedy for scarring over burns. One ounce each of litharge, white lead, and very finely ground burnt barley, three ounces of wax, nine ounces of rose oil or myrtle oil; melt the wax with the oil, sprinkle in the finely ground burnt barley, and combine; then grind the litharge and white lead in a mortar with wine, take it up, and use.
On those whose internal organs have been drawn out, and if the intestines protrude from a wound. For a tear or a laceration. When a laceration—
—or tear occurs, nothing else helps but polemonia.
On animals suffering from ravenous hunger.

By Hierocles. For the animal suffering from ravenous hunger, we too say the same as stated above. But if it is from starvation, and so on; or drench with egg yolks in wine, or likewise with spelt-groats in wine. For these are the most effective remedy for them.
On animals wasting away from an unclear cause.

An antidote of Theomnestus for the same. With an antidote, and so on; or a young pig, and so on; or chestnuts, and so on; or boil rue in old wine and drench for three days, and then, after a gap of another three days, boil pennyroyal in wine and drench for another three days. And, having anointed its ‘broad sinew,’ drench again, adding old oil boiled up with rue and old lard. Then grind bay-berries fine, boil them, add wax, and anoint the animal’s broad sinew.
To make a horse fat. If you wish to fatten a horse, feed it on grain and roasted vetch and wheat-flour soaked in water. For it puts on flesh this way and is roused to mating.
On making animals well-nourished and vigorous. Sprinkle the chaff or the fodder that the animals eat with wine-and-brine.

Another remedy of Pelagonius for maintaining a horse’s good condition. After the horse has regained its bodily fat from the food described above, it should be fed on beans and barley. For one must take care to keep horses’ bodies whole and sound. We shall preserve this in the following way: let it be rubbed down by hand every day,

which contributes greatly to the good condition of the body and feet, and at a suitable time let it be brought to exercise, to the manger, and to drink. If the animal has become chilled on the road, once it has been brought into the stable, it should be warmed, and its loins anointed with warm oil, while its head and back should be anointed with lard and oil.

For weakness and fatigue the remedy is rest, so that it may sleep gently, and that oil or lard mixed with wine be put into its throat. If it has become overheated, wash its nostrils and face with vinegar-and-water mixed with pennyroyal, and put three eggs mixed with wine into its throat. Above all, care must be taken that there is no dampness in the stable, but that it stands in a dry place. For dampness ruins its hooves — which we shall easily avoid if the flooring of the stable is of oak and kept clean.

If, after all this careful attention and feeding, the horse’s leanness persists, know that it is being harmed at night by some wind, and is thereby afflicted with various colics. One must help it, as Cornelius Celsus advises, by burning and grinding dog bones, mixing them with old lard, forming them into little balls, and putting an odd number of these into its throat with wine for three days, and by fumigating the place where it stands with unfired sulphur.
A compound for a horse. Ten pounds each of pine-nuts, almonds, raisins, dried figs, pistachios, and dates, saffron,

clove, spikenard, dried ginger, tragacanth, hyssop, and marjoram, five ounces each, pepper and trypsidion, two and a half ounces each. One must soak the tragacanth beforehand in must, and likewise grind the saffron with sweet wine, and knead it all together.

On an unclear affliction. Nearly all the afflictions of dumb animals are unclear. If, then, you wish to treat whatever affliction is present in the animal, whatever it may be, pour ground silphium with dark unmixed wine into the nostrils, and every unclear affliction will be treated.
On mange, leprosy, lichen, and vitiligo.

Pelagonius’s remedy for the same. An herb, and so on; or old urine sediment, and so on; or the plant called the ‘mange-plant,’ which is found dry like mange itself: grind this while dry, and mix in cedar-resin and oil with liquid pitch, and anoint it in the sun.
Another remedy, that of Choricoius. Chop and mix in equal parts olive bark, asphalt, sulphur, calamint, and pig dung with old oil, and use — a very good remedy. Or frogs, and so on.
From Dioscorides. Mastic-tree oil cures mange in dogs and other animals.
Another way, so as to grow hair the same day. Boil green horehound with myrrh-oil, and grind until it has the consistency of an ointment, and smear on.

Another tested remedy. Distilled soap-lye, sulphur, storax-gum, wild raisins; mix both together, and apply by hand while the remedy is cold, in the sun. Or pig urine with its filth, or this: first wash the hide
with soap, burn straw to make lye, and, having anointed the hide with oil, sprinkle the lye on up to a third time.
For every kind of animal. Melt unsalted pig lard, grind sulphur, mix and warm it, add bay oil, and, warming it again, smear it on.
For mange in goats. Make stakes of cherry-wood branches and fix them inside the pen all around. For by scratching against these the goats become healthy.
For mange in horses and oxen. Boil olive-lees and mix in an equal amount of cedar-resin, and smear on.
For dogs. Mange-sulphur, litharge, wild raisins, vinegar and boy’s urine; or burn the alkanet plant, boil it with oil, and anoint with the lees.
By Africanus. The body of the sea-urchin, smeared on a mangy body, makes it well.

A preparation for mange. Mange-sulphur, storax-gum, wild raisins, the urine of a boy seven or eight years old, soap; grind the dry ingredients, mix, and anoint the mangy horse — in summer in the sun, in winter in the warm parts of the bath. Let it first be scraped with a currycomb or a potsherd until it draws blood, and then anointed. If the mange occurs in winter, use only the mange-sulphur, urine, and soap, but in summer one must use the whole preparation described above.

Another way. Grind three ounces of litharge and one and a half ounces one and a half hexagia of green rue leaves together, add three ounces of myrtle oil, and, grinding them together, anoint the places with feathers.

Another way, a remarkable mange remedy. Two ounces each of white lead, litharge, unfired sulphur, and wax; soak two fresh eggs in vinegar for a day and a night, then grind them, shells and all, and mix well with the ground dry ingredients. Then melt the wax with one and a half ounces of rose oil, combine, and use, applying it in the sun or by a charcoal fire. Or one ounce each of rosin, unfired sulphur, and black pitch, four ounces of wax, one ounce of oil, eight onions, enough vinegar; boil the onions with the oil, discard them, and add the rest, and use.
For lichen. Chop white poplar and mullein and apply as a poultice all around the aching place while the moon is waning, and bandage it.
For lichen and mange. One ounce each of asphalt, unfired sulphur, and manna, two ounces of verdigris, one ounce of pumice, enough vinegar. Use in the sun or by a fire.
For moist lichen. One ounce each of unfired sulphur and rue, two ounces of wax, one ounce of myrtle oil.

For lichen. Eighteen carats each of unfired sulphur and frankincense, one and a half hexagia of gum, one hexagion three carats of aloe, one and a half hexagia of acacia gum; take up in vinegar. If you wish it more effective, add more sulphur.
Or grind garlic well with unfired sulphur and smear on.
For wild lichen. Mix two ounces each of asphodel root, unfired sulphur, and manna with sharp vinegar, and use.
For dark vitiligo patches. Ground marshmallow seed smeared on with vinegar.
Another way, a tested remedy for white and dark vitiligo. Myrrh, unfired sulphur, soda-foam, white hellebore,
and burnt sea-anemone. Use boldly, in the sun, with vinegar.
The difference between mange and leprosy. Leprosy differs from mange in that in mange certain bran-like flakes appear stuck to the skin, whereas in leprosy the skin is like the scales of large fish.

For leprosy, then, most of the remedies already given are helpful, but these especially: one ounce each of bull-hide glue, sage, and the tear-gum of the wild olive, two ounces each of caper-root bark and gum; grind these with vinegar, knead, and use, anointing in the sun, having first cleansed the place.
A tested treatment for vitiligo. Mix equal parts of unfired sulphur and litharge and use.
For white and dark vitiligo. It is called ‘alphos’ from changing color — for the ancients called changing ‘alphainein.’ Smear on equal parts of fig leaves, unfired sulphur, and alum with vinegar.

For leprosy. For those troubled by leprosy, the first fitting remedy is purging the body from both directions. Chill pig’s blood and grind it very fine with liver-colored aloe and myrrh in old wine, and drench with it, and use the mange compound for the affected areas, and the disease will be checked. Vulture’s blood, ground together with black chamaeleon-thistle root and cedar-resin and smeared on, clears leprosy, with beet leaves or cabbage applied on top.
Another tested remedy. One and a half ounces of cardamom seed, one ounce of blue vitriol, half an ounce each of unfired sulphur and split and round alum,
grind carefully with vinegar and anoint in the sun, having first cleansed the place with vinegar and niter.
To treat white leprosy without a scalpel. Chop mullein
On inflammation of the bones.

For inflammations and gatherings of what are called the salivary glands. One ounce each of fern root, reed, marshmallow, African fig, cypress-balls, sea-balls, soda-foam, iris, wax, and calcined bones; chop all these and bind them onto the animal’s knees, and you will heal it without the use of a blade.
For every kind of inflammation. Burn the shells of sea-mussels, grind the ash with wine, and anoint the places; for it draws the inflammation out from deep within and relieves the pain.
To prevent a wound from becoming inflamed. Soak water-and-oil in a wad of wool and apply, or wine-and-oil.

For inflammations. Repellent remedies, suited to inflammations just beginning, are horned poppy, pellitory-of-the-wall, parsley-piert, water-crowfoot, plantain, knotgrass, houseleek, and the like. Soothing remedies, suited to inflammations at their height, are mallow, roasted and applied as a poultice with bread and a little rose oil. Excellent too is melilot boiled in must and applied as a poultice with bread, and dates soaked in must with bread and rose oil.
In the decline of the inflammation, best is wild mallow applied as a poultice with bread, and raisins with their pips removed, with a little bread
and honey, and barley meal applied as a poultice with honey alone.

A repellent and anti-inflammatory remedy for old inflammation and swelling. Grind comfrey, amaranth, and sow-thistle, and add to the broth rose-water, saffron, camphor, and egg whites. Then take genuine sandalwood, rub it down in a genuine earthenware vessel soaked from outside, and gather the moist rubbings from both the sandalwood and the vessel, as much as will be enough, and, mixing it all together, anoint the affected place repeatedly, and you will quickly disperse it — for it works excellently.
On wounds in hollow places.
On animals that have fallen down a cliff or into a ditch.
On kicking or biting by a horse.
On fracture.

For a sprained fetlock. If a horse’s foot is sprained, treat it thus: foment with warm water and rub with pig fat, together with the feet and shins, and apply a sponge soaked in water to the shin for four days.

Then prepare a soft plaster of this kind: three ounces each of white dried figs, goat fat, and alum, half an ounce of roasted niter; grind these and soften with old oil and bandage on, having first fomented the place with warm water, and stand it in a place where there is cold water.
And when it comes out of the cold, foment it and apply the remedy again, or mix southernwood with wine, and apply twice a day.
By Africanus. Dog’s brain sets a fracture in
fourteen days, smeared on linen and applied, with wool wrapped over it.
A plaster for the fetlock. Mastic, myrrh-frankincense, bdellium, sagapenum gum, sarcocolla, and aloe, ground with vinegar.

A cauterizing soft plaster, effective also for bruises. Two ounces each of Tyrrhenian wax, Attic propolis, manna, mistletoe-gum, Spanish opium, storax, and bdellium; four ounces of bay-berries; four ounces each of Bruttian pitch, turpentine resin, and African resin; one ounce each of stag marrow and goat fat. Pound the bay-berries and boil them with the rest, and use it on fractures. And if you do not wish to cauterize with iron, use it this way and leave it on for days, so that it may take effect. Keep what is left over, and whenever you wish, warm it and use it on the kidneys, hips, and joints.

Moschion’s fracture remedy, for fractures with or without a wound, from Heraclides. One and a half ounces each of dry pitch, litharge, and calf fat; nine ounces each of manna, mulberry sap, and castor oil or old oil; two ounces two ounces of Tyrrhenian wax; one ounce each of opopanax, scraped verdigris, henna oil, copper, and galbanum; four and a half ounces of liquid pitch; two ounces three ounces of turpentine; five ounces of vinegar.

Another plaster. One ounce each of litharge, pitch, and calf lard; five ounces of wax; two ounces of burnt verdigris; ten ounces each of turpentine [and something lost]; nine ounces of mastic oil; one ounce one and a half hexagia of galbanum; one ounce of opopanax; enough vinegar.
On moist and dry cholera.
A preliminary drink for purging bile. Five ounces of old wine—
—one and a half ounces of good oil, two ounces three ounces of honey, one ounce of pepper; use with pressed grapes.

On those suffering from cholera. Take a bunch of fruiting leeks, chop the heads, and press out the juice. Then boil green barley, press out its liquid, mix it with the leek juice, boil it, and give a spoonful to drink.
On carcinoma. For carcinomas of the eyes. Vetch, and so on; or grind the ash of a burnt sea-crab, very fine, with very fine cadmia, knead with oil, and apply. It helps greatly.

A soothing remedy for ulcerated carcinomas. One ounce each of litharge, wax, and pig fat, egg yolks boiled in hot ashes, nine ounces of oil, half an ounce each of myrrh, iris, and birthwort. Grind the litharge with water and a little oil, then add the eggs and grind together, then chop the rest fine, melt the wax with the fat and oil, mix it all together, and anoint linen or wool pledgets and apply to the sore, and you will heal it painlessly.

Another way. Carcinomas in a fold of skin (for they vary) are treated by human serum mixed with stag marrow and lion fat with rose oil, applied as a pessary. But those on the udders grow worse the more they are treated.
On sebaceous cysts and all growths.
A plaster for sebaceous cysts, for every affliction. One ounce of litharge, ammoniac gum, galbanum, opopanax, burnt copper, copper scale, split alum, sa-
-gapenum gum, Phrygian stone, Colophonian resin, myrrh, and castoreum, one carat each, nine ounces of old oil.

Apsyrtus, on sebaceous cysts. The sebaceous cyst forms on the hind legs, in the hocks, inside and outside, like an egg. If it is recent, make an incision from the outer side, not a large one, just enough for the fluid to drain out. It will flow out like honey. When you have pressed this out well, use the wound-remedy, and on the outside a soft plaster, until it heals. But if the cyst becomes hard despite the soft plaster, use the cautery, encircling the inner part properly, not obliquely, and when the scabs fall off, use the wound-remedy and vetch-meal, until it heals.

If sebaceous cysts form on a horse’s hocks. Sebaceous cysts form in the middle of the hocks. Apply as a poultice the lees of fragrant wine with Cimolian earth, having first fomented the place. If it does not respond, one must cauterize with irons.

On the wasp-sting-like swelling. If such swellings occur on a bare part of the body, they should be removed with a scalpel, or better cauterized with the iron, as Apsyrtus thinks. But if they occur in fleshy parts, do not use either the scalpel or the cautery; instead chop bramble shoots, knead with vinegar, and bandage on, until it scars over. The anthedon resembles the sting of wild bees.
A tested decoction for every inflammation and hardness. Knead goat dung and wheat flour with vinegar and must-syrup, and use.
A poultice for a spontaneous swelling. Boil one ounce each of pitch, asphalt, and manna with one ounce of wine, and apply as a poultice; or chop winter-cherry with oil and apply.

A plaster effective against every hardness and fractures of joints and ribs, that dissolves strangulated hernias, scrofulous swellings, tumors, fistulas in sores, chronic sores and those from animal bites; it treats dropsical patients, draws out splinters and thorns excellently, and works for those with spleen, liver, and foot-gout complaints, especially those with flux. Three ounces each of litharge, white lead, scraped verdigris, turpentine, Gallic stone, iron-scale stone, Assian stone, split alum, and myrobalan, two ounces of copper scale, two and a half ounces each of yellow wax, dry pitch, and male frankincense, eight ounces of Judean asphalt, three ounces of old oil; grind the dry ingredients with vinegar in a mortar until it has the consistency of an ointment, then melt the meltable ingredients and pour them in, and, having kneaded it together, use.
The yellow plaster for hard swellings. Three ounces of resin, one and a half ounces of wax, five ounces of orpiment, five ounces of storax, five ounces of ammoniac gum, and enough vinegar.

A plaster that dries up varicose veins painlessly and cures them without fail. One ounce each of asphalt and unfired sulphur, eight ounces of very old oil, seven ounces of liquid turpentine. Break the asphalt into chickpea-sized pieces and boil it with the oil, without stirring, until it melts. Then add the turpentine and boil until it no longer stains, and, taking it off the fire, sprinkle in the very finely ground sulphur, and, combining it, pour it into a mortar—
—containing cold water, and, having kneaded it, use.
For a splinter.
For an embedded thorn, glass, or nail.
Roast onions in hot ashes, crush them, and apply hot, and bandage, changing it over three days.
On figs, ant-warts, skin-tags, and red ‘thymes.’
By Africanus, on figs, ant-warts, and skin-tags.

Ant-warts are outgrowths on the body resembling rough nail-heads; they occur in many people in many places. People call this affliction ‘myrmekiai,’ which many superstitious people take as a sign of something about to happen to them.

Their removal is various, and all methods have been tried. Some, watching for someone to urinate on the ground, kneaded the resulting mud and applied it to the place, thereby shutting the cause in with the mud.
Others, grinding squirting-cucumber and applying it, got rid of them this way.
Or, gathering the flower of chicory (properly called heliotrope) before sunrise, trace around the place three times, and the wart will stop.

For figs on the heels. It occurs, and so on; first excise it, and so on; or burn a preserved sea-bream’s head with vinegar and smear on; or take the sap dripping from burning green vine-shoots, knead it with sheep dung and a little vinegar, and apply.
Heraclides of Tarentum’s remedy for chronic ant-warts.

Grind equal parts of unfired sulphur, realgar, and galbanum with vinegar and form into lozenges. When needed, dissolve in vinegar and smear on. One must add an equal amount of squirting-cucumber, and cut—

—around the wart with a scalpel in a circle, and then smear on the remedy. Or combine equal parts of burnt fresh wine-lees, lime, and verdigris, and use — for it removes the wart at once. Once it has fallen off, treat it as an ordinary sore.

A tested remedy for skin-tags. Burn vine-shoots, knead with the urine of an uncorrupted child, and apply. Or take a spider’s web thread from the trees, wind it around, and they will fall off; or bind on the scrapings of green gourds, and they will fall off.
For figs and ant-warts growing on a stalk. Grind Gangra salt, sprinkle it on, and bind it up, keeping it lifted with some strong support. Do this daily and it will heal.

A remedy that consumes and dries up ant-warts, ‘thymes,’ and skin-tags. One ounce each of split alum, roasted blue vitriol, and bull-hide glue, two ounces of copper scale. Grind the dry ingredients, mix with the bull-hide glue dissolved in vinegar, and smear on.
By Africanus. If you hide a snake’s shed skin in dates and feed it to any animal as a morsel, you will clear away its skin-tags.
On clots.

Hierocles, on clots. Clots occur in the most sensitive places, like swellings full of blood or pus. Cauterize them with straight irons, then anoint the place with salt and oil, and for the following seven days with grease. If the scabs fall off, cleanse the wound and treat it as after cauterization.
On sinew afflictions and for wounds affecting the sinews.

A poultice for a severed sinew. Chop barley roots, earthworms, snails, manna, and lard, or lime and Sinopian earth, and use. Or twenty ounces of vinegar, one ounce of rich pitch, three ounces of opopanax; dissolve the opopanax in the vinegar and melt the pitch, and combine. This is suitable for punctured sinews. Or one ounce of cinnamon, one ounce each of dittany, fennel, and turpentine, two ounces of marjoram, eight ounces of wax, ten ounces of balsam-sap.

For irritation of the sinews from running. Mix equal parts of pollen and lime with honey and apply as a poultice; on the third day, undo it and foment with the juice of linseed and fenugreek, until it is thinned, then bleed it, and it recovers.

An excellent tested plaster for the ankles and flat sinews. One ounce each of bull’s gall, bulbs, and snails, nine ounces of fine wheat flour. Boil the bull’s gall in wine, and the rest in order. Then pound sumac and calamint together and add them.

For exposed sinews. Nine ounces of perfumer’s wax, twelve ounces of spikenard ointment or foliated nard-oil or nard, one ounce of zinc oxide, one ounce each of spikenard, cardamom, and malabathrum leaf.
A fomentation for old sinew troubles. Tree-mallow, niter, wine, green mistletoe, unfired sulphur, butter, Cyrenaic sap; mix with vinegar and foment for three days, and pour it on.
A relaxing poultice for the sinews. Chop pine-nuts, raisins, and opopanax carefully, each on its own, combine, and use.
For wounds of the sinews. Warm water, though—
—the most fitting remedy for other inflammations, is the worst enemy for a sinew-wound: for putrefaction arises in such conditions from moistening and warming remedies together.

It is better, then, to treat sinew-wounds with thin oil that has no astringency, and better still if it is two or three years old; for the treatment of the wounded part requires remedies that raise heat, are sufficiently drying, and are, by the fineness of their substance, very penetrating — for only such remedies can draw the discharge up from deep within without straining or biting the tissues.

For this reason it is fitting to boil dill and rue in oil and pour it, as hot as possible, over the place for a long while, or to melt the spurge wax-salve or the ‘invincible’ plaster with a little oil and anoint with it; or apply the same plaster and lay soft wool soaked in warm oil on top of the plaster; undo it twice or three times a day.

It is also fitting to soak the underlying areas of the armpits and neck continually with plenty of warm oil; and if it concerns the sinews of the leg or the punctured groins, one must soak the whole spine and neck continually with much warm oil. When sinew-wounds are badly treated from the start, inflammation and putrefaction follow; one must therefore use poultices of this kind: bean-meal or vetch-meal boiled in distilled lye with oxymel, without oil — for this remedy is very good for those—
—and so on. Take up peach leaves, centaury, and southernwood with old human urine, and use.

By Africanus. To expel worms with unmedicated enemas, plain water is enough for me, taken in this way: dip the thumb and forefinger of the left hand repeatedly into the stream of an untroubled spring, and sprinkle the affected, worm-ridden place three times. The worms will all come out, following one another, with none left inside.
If you wish to kill wild lice. If they are inside, and so on, in the sun; or use cedar-resin, green caper leaves, and leeks likewise.
On intestinal worms, by Apsyrtus. Boil pomegranate-rind leaves with rose oil and vinegar, and use.
For flat worms. Drench with equal parts of niter, cress seed, and pepper with must-syrup.

On worm-infestation. Worm-infestation is the most severe and incurable of all afflictions, and can defeat every remedy there is. It is recognized when the animal is repeatedly seized by pain and rolls on the ground. It is treated thus: pour four ounces of oil and half an ounce of pitch into the nostrils, and you will expel dead worms through the mouth.

On pinworms — this also works on humans. I learned from a suggestion put to us by Velmus Tryphon, a physician of Thessalonica, that against the flat creatures that form in the liver of animals — which occur not only in the liver but sometimes also in the stomach, and not only in

four-footed animals, but also in humans — quite beneficial are the administration of oil and filed ivory shavings, ground and drenched with warm water, likewise filings of stag horn, and black cummin, which some call ‘black seed,’ the kind sprinkled on bread. The plant called wormwort, chopped and smeared on, works especially well, and likewise peach leaves given as a drench. Also very effective is applying water-and-oil continually to the belly as a fomentation, for the worms will be driven away, so that they do not travel to the upper passages but descend to the rectum instead. For it is said that worms make their way out not only through the mouth or nostrils, but sometimes even through the ears and eyes.

On lice in the mouth. You will recognize lice-infestation in the mouth thus, and so on; or soak pledgets in the spittle of a fasting man and apply. For it also kills worms in the ears and makes scars match the surrounding skin color.

On intestinal worms. Liver-colored aloe drenched with cold water. Or chop and sift dry hemp seed, make it into a juice with water, press it through a cloth, and drench with six ounces. Or grind half an ounce each of Pontic wormwood, fenugreek, and lettuce-seed, nine grains of dry lupine, one ounce of parsley, with honey, and drench.
By Africanus. That the donkey, alone of all animals, carries neither lice nor ticks.
On those bitten by vipers, and the rest of the venomous creatures and caterpillars.
On the buprestis-beetle and the rest. Soak the flowering fruit of the wild fig-tree—
—in water and pour it into the nostrils.
On the shrew-mouse. If a shrew-mouse bites, and so on; or chop buckthorn leaves with lard and apply as a poultice, or pound chaste-tree fruit with vinegar.

By Africanus, on those bitten by mad dogs, on hydrophobia, and on the rest of the bites of creeping things. The present drench has four ingredients: gentian, myrrh, round birthwort, and bay-berries. Chop and sift these in equal parts, and take them up with raw honey. The dose is the size of an Egyptian bean. Give it to those bitten by snakes in water, to those stung by scorpions in first-run wine, over the course of three days.

By the same author. The treatment for the bite of asps: taking a great many bed-bugs is believed to be a very great remedy for those bitten by asps, or turtle’s urine, drunk and also dropped onto the bite, either by itself or with many bed-bugs. The physician Phobius, for those bitten by asps, gave what is called ‘the hemorrhoid’ — roasting and grinding the snake itself and giving it to drink in wine — and conversely he said that those bitten by the ‘hemorrhoid’ snake should likewise use asp in the same way. He said that Inaros the Libyan had handed down this remedy, that each is the cure for the other.

An easily obtained antidote of the same author. Twenty rue leaves, two royal walnuts, one lump of salt, two dried figs, given beforehand to a fasting horse as a drench, will make it so that it cannot be harmed by any poison or other venomous creature. And so that it may not be stung by a scorpion, write on a tin plate: ‘Abbas,’ and bind this around the animal’s neck, and it will not be stung by a scorpion.

A remedy for snake-bite and the rest, and for rabies. Give perfumed wine to drink, and, grinding a morsel of bread with goat lard, taking it up with warm water, put it in a heated earthenware dish, and, kneading it together, anoint.

For those bitten by vipers. Cut off the viper’s own head, and, holding it securely with tongs, apply it to the bite while the cut of the neck is still warm, and it will draw out the venom. Or cut open a bird and apply it warm to the bite, and change it repeatedly before it dries out, and you will heal it.

A tested remedy for those bitten by wild beasts. Chop and sift St. John’s wort and give as a drench. Or chop green spurge and apply to the bite, dripping on its sap too; or grind green hemlock leaves together with their seed with old wine and apply as a poultice to the bite.
By Africanus, for the bite of any wild creature. Grind cress and apply as a plaster with linen, or its seed
soaked and ground likewise, applied with linen.

By the same author, a non-inflaming remedy for the sting of venomous water creatures. Lemnian earth is suited to the stings of venomous sea creatures, given with wine, and white mountain-clay applied as a poultice with vinegar heals similarly.

By the same author, a preventive so as not to be harmed by any venomous bite. Two ounces of raw-pressed oil, four ounces of freshly slaughtered stag marrow, enough wax; melt both together, strain, and use against all venomous creatures as needed.
By the same author, on the centipede. The centipede—

—does greater harm. But you, having smeared on some of the theriac antidote, heal the stung place. The fruit and flowers of asphodel, drunk with wine, are the counter-remedy to centipedes, and unripe figs applied as a poultice with wine and vetch relieve the pain.

By the same author, on spiders. There are many kinds of spiders. Two of them are capable of doing harm: the ‘raving’ spider and the ‘bronze’ spider. For those stung by the raving spider, grind four ounces four hexagia of hyssop or marjoram with an equal amount of roasted salt and apply with honey. Or give a drench of as much cumin as three fingers can hold, together with an equal amount of chaste-tree fruit, in three ounces of wine. One should also give barley-cakes and garlic, and something taken through the mouth is beneficial.

By the same author, against bees. Against stinging insects — wasps, bees, hornets, sawflies, bumblebees, and wood-wasps — apply bay leaves as a poultice, or mallow, or mint, or coriander. Cow dung smeared on also works, as does fig-tree sap with mulberry leaves, or calamint, or lentils smeared on with oil. Animals remain unstung if wild-cucumber root boiled together with oil is used, whence one should anoint them with galbanum and oil. This too, fumigated before the hives are opened, likewise keeps them unstung; or grind balm-leaf with oil and anoint, or fumigate with cow dung or sage. Every stinging insect is killed when sprinkled with oil.
By the same author, on the dipsas. The dipsas too has many names. It is called ‘kausōn’ [the burner] and ‘prēstēr’ [the blaster] from the effects it—

—produces, and ‘melanouros’ [black-tail] and ‘ammodytes’ [sand-diver] from its habitat and its own appearance — a creature smaller than the viper and more dangerous. For it produces in those it bites burning heat and such extreme thirst that they burst apart from drinking. For the bite of the dipsas, a drench of galingale in wine and water helps, as does ground ladanum given in wine, and also the citron, the western fruit so called, given beforehand as a counter-remedy, or given after as an aid — especially the golden-colored kind.

On the oak-snake. The oak-snake, which makes its home among the roots of oaks and coils around other trees as well, is so harmful and destructive that if anyone should tread on it, the feet are stripped of skin and swellings form over the whole leg. And still more remarkable: even if someone tries to treat these victims, that person’s own hands are stripped of skin and swellings form over the whole leg. The juice of ash-tree leaves, drunk before any food or drink, is very useful as a drench.

By the same author, on various bites and stings. Particular remedies for the bites and stings of venomous creatures have already been given; these are the general ones: iris drunk with vinegar, Christ’s-thorn seed or myrtle juice with wine, cardamom likewise, or pear fruit or half an ounce of trefoil, two hexagia six carats of asphodel root with wine, and silphium sap or barley seed, a drench of a germander decoction, and centaury, dittany, castoreum, rue, sage, calamint,

and chaste-tree. In addition to these, apply also a poultice of bran with vinegar or wine, or radishes or bulbs. Having said this much, many others have added further remedies, each praising by experience what he found effective.

In addition to these, one man had the patient drink leek juice, another took the brain of a live hen, mixed it with unmixed wine, and gave it to the one in danger; another mixed a boy’s urine with wine and likewise gave it. Another cut open a mouse and applied it to the sting, and it drew the venom into the mouse.

But I myself prefer, above the many remedies, the one I set out for those bitten by mad dogs and stung by scorpions — the Parthian mystery-remedy, made from four equal parts: myrrh, birthwort, gentian, and bay-berry. Take these, then, grind them with wine, bring to a boil, and drench. Also easily obtained are these: goat’s milk given alone or with wine, and frogs boiled in wine and drenched together with the wine they were boiled in, for all venomous bites and toads.

And ground southernwood with wine, likewise agaric and chaste-tree fruit likewise, Ethiopian cumin and Italian cumin drenched with wine, and wild leek eaten, bay leaves ground and drenched with wine or water, or acorns eaten are suitable, and bed-bug seed, mandrake root with honey-water. Leeches applied to the bite also help and draw out the venom. Goat dung with marjoram applied helps those struck by venomous creatures, as does dried elephant dung. And chaste-tree
leaves applied as a poultice, and barley-meal likewise drenched abundantly with wine-lees and dry wine or seawater, are suited to all venomous creatures that kill by chilling.

Whatever creature has bitten, then, take its head and apply it to the bites, and, bandaging it, you will heal without inflammation. Or burn the head of the creature that struck, and apply the ash. Or grind dragon-arum root (that is, wild arum) and apply it to the struck place, having first scarified it. Hyacinth juice, given as a drench, is the counter-remedy to every venomous creature. The root of the wild grape-vine worn as an amulet, and its fruit given as a drench, is suited to every bite and sting of venomous creatures.
A fomentation for every bite of a venomous creature. Eighteen carats each of birthwort, rue, and trefoil, nine carats of wild carrot; soak in water and foment.

On henbane. For a horse that has gorged on henbane, woman’s milk given as a drench helps, and likewise warm donkey’s milk, and further wormwood with wine and pepper, and mint likewise with wine. Cow’s milk alone, given as a drench, counters all these, or goat’s milk. Hen broth with oil, and lamb’s blood boiled with honey-water, and purslane juice combined with honey-water to the consistency of an ointment, all help. Pine-nuts and cucumber seed drenched with wine work together for recovery.
A lozenge of Anthemystion, for every bite of creeping and venomous creatures. One hexagion of castoreum,

ammi fruit, one ounce each of trefoil, two ounces of bryony, two ounces of anise, one ounce of vetch-meal; foment with wine. Good too is the remedy from the theriac vine, as will be set out among the most important remedies; grind it, shape it into a lozenge, give it beforehand as a drink, and, dissolving it with wine, smear it on.

A remedy of Asclepiades for bleeding wounds from the bites of bears and leopards, and for severed sinews. One ounce each of scraped verdigris and round alum, one ounce each of copper scale and galbanum, sixteen ounces of wax, thirty-two ounces of pine-resin, one ounce of oil. Grind the dry ingredients and the galbanum with vinegar, and, melting the meltable ones, pour it in.
On those bitten by cats. Melt turpentine with honey and oil, and use, or grind centaury with honey, or grind fresh chicken dung with poultry fat, and use.

A fumigation of Strato that drives away venomous creatures. One ounce each of galbanum, spelt root, stag horn, and black cummin; grind them all with vinegar and shape into lozenges, and, when needed, soak them in oil and fumigate the middle of the house, or the burrow through a funnel.
For the sting of a sea-stingray. The mullet fish, split open while still alive and applied to the site of the sting, provides immediate healing.

By Africanus, so that draught animals are not harmed at night by a toad lurking in the dark and puffing itself against them. The toad is accustomed to puff itself most dangerously against draught animals, if it happens unnoticed at night in a stable or a dark place, and diseases follow from this—

—pestilential to their life, and swellings hard to cure, so that every remedy proves useless against the danger. To prevent it from ever doing this, one must keep a fire continually burning in the stables. For this creature, as proof against itself, fears fire.
On leeches.
For leeches stuck in the mouth. Crush five bed-bugs, and so on; or drench with a cup of fish-sauce, tested by experience.
On ornithia.

[lacuna] into bird dung or a feather, or it will pull out fine, mucous droppings. It is helped thus: take the solid dung of a hen and grind it. Then mix in six ounces of wheat meal and one ounce of sumac, knead with dark wine, form into cakes, and give it to eat with wheat chaff.

But if it is loose in another way, take six ounces of wheat meal and an equal amount of crushed grape-pips, mix them together, and, having boiled buckthorn in dry wine and mixed it in, give as a sufficient drench. Do not give it barley to eat until it stops. For this will be the cure for the affliction. And if it has also been poisoned, grind coriander and radish root in wine and drench. Excellent too is ground ‘enitzin’ drenched with wine.
On wild cabbage, mouse-bane, hemlock, and hellebore.
On hemlock. Drench with fresh-drawn donkey’s or cow’s milk and wormwood together with pepper and rue.
On kentritis.
By Hierocles. These are the signs of kentritis: the body itches beneath the skin and is full of distress, and it gnaws at itself, and

—is sensitive to the affliction and to the itching. It is treated thus: draw blood from the shoulders or the groins, and mix into it unfired sulphur, oil, vinegar, and manna. Smear this on the animal. Then anoint with gentle oil, and it recovers.
On the eruption of teeth.
How and when one must cauterize, and on cauterization.

A cauterizing remedy that dries moist places, tightens loose and spongy tissue, restores exhausted parts, and strengthens and reinforces damaged ones. One ounce each of Judean or Apollonian asphalt, wax, and roasted resin; lard, stag marrow, Arabian bdellium, wax, propolis, opopanax, castoreum, galbanum, storax-tear, distillate, hyssop juice, ammoniac-tear, and Bruttian pitch, two ounces each; manna and frankincense, six ounces each; four ounces of Italian mistletoe-gum.
On cauterizing agents. Combine barley meal, bran, egg, a little vinegar, and rose oil, and use.
For burns. Boil apple bark in water, apply, and you will marvel.
Another way. Two ounces each of propolis, ammoniac gum, opopanax, split alum, and pepper, one ounce of pine-cones, one ounce of hog’s fennel, four ounces of galbanum, one ounce of niter.
How one must feed on grass.

From Aristotle, on the same. Horses, mules, and donkeys are grain-eaters and grass-eaters, but they thrive above all on their drinking-water. For as the draught animals drink the water, so also does it go with their enjoyment of food, and whatever

grass a horse finds least disagreeable with its drinking-water, that is the more nourishing grass for it. Grass makes the coat smooth when the animal is in foal. But when it has hard awns, it is not good. As for alfalfa, the first cutting is poor, and so is any water that comes with a bad smell — for it stinks. Oxen seek to drink clean water, but horses, like camels, do not mind; the camel actually prefers to drink water that is muddy and thick. Indeed, it does not drink from rivers at all unless it first stirs them up.

How one must turn the animals in the stable out to green fodder. The one who is putting the stabled animals out to green fodder should, before releasing them onto the pasture, first attend to these treatments: blow air through the nostrils, holding the temples, with wine-and-oil, on account of the tightness of the head, and, after a gap of three days, let it bend down toward the ground — not into deep grass, but shorter grass — so that, with the straining of the sense of smell and the movement the head undergoes, it may pass off through the nostrils all the ill humor of the sickness from the brain. After three days, bleed it from the neck, taking care because the veins there are the jugulars. It is necessary to bleed from those particular places, for all the channels lodged in the animal lead up to them.

And, having bled it, anoint it with the blood itself, with due care, and stand it in deep darkness for seven days, giving it the grass to eat; then cleanse it, and, having sponged away the moisture of the water, blow wine over its whole

body, and rub it down lightly with fine salt because of excessive salivation, and let it graze on every kind of pasture alone. Drench it, once it is on the grass, with cooling remedies made with good must, and it will be healthy for good. But if it coughs while on the grass, know that it is being troubled by the awns of the grass. Especially, then, when—

—the grass runs out, the windpipe becomes clogged by the awns and brings on the cough. For this reason one must treat it with the ‘bull remedy,’ soaking the bull’s-pizzle preparation in honeyed wine, so as to cleanse the windpipe.

Apsyrtus to the general Ursus, greetings. You asked me, my lord Ursus, wondering how sores form on horses’ feet, and what these signify. It is this: whenever it happens that a riding-horse comes under a rider who does not have secure skill in sitting and guiding the animal, but drives it in a scattered way, being carried around—

—in this way, because it is not properly guided by the rider’s skill, it throws its legs sideways as it plants its hooves, and, as the joints are shaken and the sinews strained, in just those places the sores and ruptures occur, along with swelling and inflammation.
It ought, then, to be—
—fomented with the prescribed relaxing remedy — better still

if seawater is available for boiling the herbs; if not, put salt into fresh water, and boil it down likewise to a third, and use it for the fomentation, and, having wiped off the moisture of the water, take it up with wine and apply as a poultice, with a raw dissolution at first, until the swellings subside. Or, taking up the remedy, having first rubbed it down with wine, apply as a poultice until the sinewy places subside. And then use phlebotomy from the visible places, and, when it walks about healthy, bind it tight with a dry soft plaster, until all the sinews regain their tone.

On tenderness of the hooves. Put a live lizard into a pot with very sharp vinegar and boil until it dissolves. Then add asphodel to the asphalt, unfired sulphur, buffalo fat and bull’s or goat’s fat, and wax and oil, and boil together. Then smear it on the soles in this way.

On bruises, and how they arise. When the stable footing is not clean, but dark and damp, the soles become inflamed and displaced, and the discharges run beneath the horn-plates, and the hooves fester as the discharges gather. Hence, when the soles are pared, they give off a purulent, foul-smelling matter. These are treated by scraping with vinegar and bran or boiled barley. The pain is severe.
On leprous feet. When a horse’s feet become leprous, one must scrape the discharge from them and treat thus: put four parts of soft alum into a small pot and pour on three parts of olive-lees—
—then heat it underneath until it boils up, and, dipping in a cloth, rub the feet with it, keeping your hand away. Do this twice a day.
On seiriasmos of a horse. Grind split orpiment with resin and anoint, or use blister-beetle with oil.
If the seiriasmos persists a long time. Knead oak ash or vine-ash with honey and smear on the feet.
Astringents for the hoof, also for mangy ones. Boil equal parts of sumac and pine in vinegar in a new pot, and, soaking a sponge with vinegar, apply. This also treats mangy hooves.
For a cracked hoof. Chop dried figs with salt and apply to the hooves.
Tiberius’s remedy for suppuration of the toes, if for some reason it is bruised and gathers fluid. Pollen, and so on.
For chafed feet. Six ounces each of liquid pitch, alum, and vinegar, enough fig leaves. Chop them all together separately, and anoint the feet of the ailing horse daily, and use as a tested remedy.

For seiriasmos. There are three kinds of seiriasmos. One kind produces dry scales and blisters on the horse’s foot and it becomes bloodied, because the condition is dry. The other kind, know, makes it bristle and discharge moisture, because it comes from a flux, and it must be treated thus: anoint the foot with ointment and leave it for one day, and after this take ground split alum, mustard, vetch-meal, and verdigris, and, mixing them all together with honey, take it up, and, having anointed the foot, bandage it.

Another way. Take plain, unsalted pig lard and sharp vinegar and mercury, and combine both strongly until they become one substance; put them into a mortar and add ground bark of green dock root, sulphur, pitch, and wild raisins. This is very useful.

Another way. First anoint the horse’s foot and rub it with a haircloth rag and vinegar, until blood comes out. Then grind glass, sift it, split a small pad, and spread the glass on it, and bind it on for three days. Then undo it, wash it with soap, and again apply another pad with glass, until it eats away and lessens the ill in the foot. And after this, apply a third pad without glass, and leave it for three days. Then wash and foment with cold water, until it heals.

Another way. Take fresh quicklime, unslaked, slake it with sharp vinegar, and spread it on a cloth, and, sprinkling on a little oil, bandage it on and leave it until the same hour the next day, then undo it. Do this until it heals.

For a tapeworm-like growth. Put liquid pitch into hot water, stir it, and pour off the hot water up to seven times. Then make it into a plaster and apply. Or knead hen dung with vinegar and, applying it, bandage it on.

A plaster for the ring-growth. One ounce each of wild raisins, unfired sulphur, ammoniac gum, myrrh, frankincense, and ladanum (that is, mastic), three ounces of resin, four hexagia each of turpentine and galbanum, two hexagia of opium, oil, wax, and soap.

Apsyrtus, on ‘goose-foot.’ A serious disease occurs in horses’ feet, around the coronet of the hooves, which causes disfigurement and lameness especially from dryness. Something like wounds and scales form above the hooves. It is treated thus: when it begins to produce wounds like scales, and grows hair not from its own natural place, but like offshoots, take an ointment and anoint the wounded place, and clean it well with a wooden knife until blood comes out. Then take bay oil and salt,

and anoint on the first day. On the next day, again cleanse the place, and take a mountain tortoise, not a marsh one, and, piercing its shell with a knife, anoint its blood on the places where the wounds are. Anoint three times a day with lard. For it marvelously both grows hair and heals the scars.
For brittle hooves. Melt butter over coals and anoint the coronet of the horse’s hooves, and let it stand in the sun. Do this for up to fifteen days and you will heal it.
For paralusis. Anoint the hoof-horn, that is, the coronet of the horse, with oil, then sprinkle unslaked lime on the place, and it recovers.

On the thigh. If the joint of the leg suffers a sprain, or a wrench, or something else happens, the leg cannot be drawn together nor can it rest, nor does it allow the hand to be brought near it. Draw blood, then, from the hock and foment—

with warm water, wine, and oil, and let it walk about. If it does not settle, cauterize similarly at the joint of the thigh itself, so that the joint area is encircled. If it still does not recover, cauterize with straight irons, taking care that the cautery does not touch the genitals.

On seirama, that is, sprain of the tendon, by the Patriarch Theophylact. Before anything else, clear the place with a depilatory, then foment with these: two ounces each of myrtle leaves, rosemary, and bay leaves; one ounce each of willow bark, bramble root, cypress-balls, asphodel root, pomegranate rind, oak-gall, and pomegranate flower, and olive-lees; two ounces of honey, enough astringent wine. Soak them all in wine for a day and night, then boil and foment by pouring on. Then, soaking a haircloth rag in vinegar with salt, rub the place until blood flows.

And take up an ointment made of: the juice of yellow acacia, resin, scraped verdigris, litharge, white lead, split orpiment, lead slag, wild raisins, blister-beetles, and liquid pitch, two ounces each; vetch-meal, roasted chickpea-meal, pomegranate rind, oak-gall, fresh lime, and ground glass, one ounce each; two and a half ounces of pig dung, the same of dog dung, nine ounces of pig fat, three ounces of seal fat. Sift them all through a fine sieve, add the fats and the liquid pitch, and, having kneaded it together, use it, spreading it on a linen rag and bandaging it on.
By Africanus, to soothe inflammations of the feet—

—and other parts. Soak seven dates beforehand in sweet wine until they are soft, and grind them very fine with enough rose oil. Then boil a little wax, fresh pig fat, and bread crumbs in equal parts with rose oil, and pour it over the ground dates, and, combining it in a mortar, make it into a moist, plaster-like paste, and apply it to the inflammation, and you will relieve it at once.
On madness, rabies, lethargy, vertigo, apiossos, epilepsy, wildness, and how to stop a mule from kicking.

On madness. It happens that a horse goes mad from the severity of pain. It shows these signs: its eyes become bloodshot, it bites and kicks itself, and runs to bite people, and dashes itself against the wall and the manger. Sometimes, too, it presses its head against the wall for a long while. One must bleed it at once from the throat and let much blood flow, and withhold all food. The next day, grind one ounce of all-heal with vinegar and give it to drink for four days, and give it leeks to eat, and bleed it again from the collarbone. If it is purged, give food and take care as needed.
On vertigo. Chop garlic and mix it with ten ounces of wine and drench through the mouth. This also helps those with difficult urination, mixing in ten egg whites too.

So that animals do not kick one another in the manger. Take clean water, wash the tail of one, and give it to the other to drink, and they will make peace. Or dissolve the dung of each in water and give it to the other to drink.
A remedy so that a wild horse travels calmly. Take a sprig of the mercury plant and wind it into the horse’s bridle.

For lethargy. When a horse is seized by this disease, it collapses, snores, sleeps excessively, and has its lip hanging loose, and yawns. Rub it down with the hands and blow wine and oil into it, and you will stop it by the seventh day.

On sleeplessness. Sores appear over its whole body as though it were mangy, and it loses its appetite, not taking food readily, and becomes dejected. Reduce its food, then, and bleed it from the neck, and drench with the lozenge made of saffron and niter, and it will be healthy. Give it also oil with saffron soaked in must.

On epilepsy. We recognize the epileptic horse by its posture: if it cannot stand, if it convulses with a groaning sound and twists its joints and lips, and sends foam through its mouth. Some of them also let out saliva. As the disease subsides, they turn livid and cannot walk straight ahead, but turn to one side, as though moved by some mechanism.

One must treat it thus: first bring it into a dark place, and bleed it according to the onset of the attack, on the first or second day. After the bloodletting, wet the head with vinegar-and-water and oil, and give relaxing food, more nourishing in strength. On the third day, take a little blood from the head, and with a small fomentation of—

—oil, continue until the fifth day. From then, foment the head thoroughly with a sponge, as much as eight or ten times, before feeding, and anoint with oil, and do this every other day, until it is healed.

By Africanus, the taming of horses. Rarely, as among men, is virtue found unmixed — so too among horses. For vice lies close to virtue, as a spiteful thing, so that the good may not appear pure. One man is eloquent, but not dignified; another commands an army, but lacks self-control. One is brave, but boastful. Another has not kept his beauty unstained, and one man has an advantage over another, yet also a fault. The same holds for the good and bad qualities found in horses. Some are rough in temper, yet passionate; good at the hunt, yet hard-mouthed; good at walking, yet insolent. Some will not accept riders, others throw them off. Some rub against walls or trees. Some are vicious by nature, others have been made so by their owners, and they bite and kick, and shy away and rear up, either hating or despising their masters. And I could name many, each ruined in a different way and by a different kind of vice, through horses.

The skills of horse-breakers, then, either check or correct these vices as far as possible: scant feeding for the insolent, gelding for the overly amorous, muzzles for the biters, wolf-tooth bits for the hard-mouthed, blows for the disobedient. But what can one do against the horse that is stubborn and will submit to no manner of persuasion, that has resolved never to obey either commands or lessons—

—for just as fully grown wild beasts, once captured, are not tamed, but even if they seem for a while to become tractable, they still do not forget their former savagery, so too this creature, once its vice has become ingrained, is hard to redirect.

Since, then, blows and threats and skill and feeding are weak against such a case, let a fault of nature be corrected by a device of nature. Let even a written charm tame it — one it will not fear, will not suspect, and by wearing which it will be subdued. In a circle around the hoof of the left forefoot, with the left hand, in left-handed writing, engrave in bronze, under a sixteen-day moon, the threat of Roman command, and it will be compelled to obedience. The writing is contained in the following pentagon, inscribed by means of this sign: phe | dolei | keso | phee | aelphchothpsylo.
Boil box-tree seed in wine and drench a mule with it for six days.
On animals unevenly matched, and on those well suited to the yoke.
On flux in the head.
On headache. Boil ivy in oil and use.
For clearing the head, pour ten ounces of fish-sauce through the nostrils.

On heaviness of the head. Bleed from the temples, especially if the eyes are running; it is also good, if from the palate, to open a third or fourth vein-like prominence, leaving alone the one near the canine tooth, since that vessel is hard to stanch. Also give a nasal remedy, and drench with cucumber-and-niter with sweet, chilled must, or a lozenge
made with sweet-flag.
A remedy for the temple. Draw blood from the temples and from the crown, and use as an anointment.
A nasal remedy to clear the head. Drench through the nostrils with ivy juice or calamint juice.
Recognizing a sound foot and a soft foot.
On sweating for no apparent cause.
For a horse sweating for no clear reason, swelling up, and repeatedly collapsing and rolling on the ground.
Take a land-frog, or whatever kind you find, remove the head, and, holding the tongue, throw it whole into the horse’s mouth; or grind two heads of garlic, dissolve in wine, and drench.
On those injured by a hobble or a tether.
On those harmed by cold.
For chilling. Drench with milk and pepper.
On gangrene and the sacred disease, that is, palpitation.
On choking from raw feeding.
For strains in the groin.

Another remedy, on groin swellings. If a swelling occurs on a horse’s chest, and sometimes it even descends to the shins of the forelegs, and afterward it becomes moist in those places and forms pus — let us cauterize the swelling at the place where it began, as quickly as possible, and on the shins too, and let us treat the sores as has been shown. But one must be wary of this affliction, because it can work its way inward to the lung and destroy the animal. Ammoniac gum softened with honey and applied disperses groin swellings, and propolis breaks them open when applied as a poultice with—
—bitter lupines and a little vinegar.
A plaster for groin swellings. Grind fenugreek very fine, mix it with unsmoked honey, and, making it into a plaster, apply it to the inflamed groin, and you will heal it most quickly and best.
For hardenings on the coronet, called ‘calluses.’
Old cheese applied with lard dissolves calluses.
How one must purge herd-animals.
On the appearance and selection of horses, on the age shown by the teeth, on the veins, and on the span of life.
By Simon of Athens, on the appearance and selection of horses.
By Simon of Athens, on the appearance and selection of horses.

It seems to me that, concerning the proper form for horsemanship, if anyone wishes to know this subject well, one must first know the horse’s native country, as — in the land of Greece, Thessaly is the best.

As for size, it admits of three descriptions: large, small, and of good size — or, if you prefer, medium — and it is clear on which of these names each case will fit. In every animal, due proportion is the best quality.

As for color, I cannot fix upon it as a mark of a horse’s excellence. Yet it seems to me that a mane which is uniform in color throughout and has especially fine hair is generally the best, or one as far removed as possible from that of the donkey or the mule.

What matters no less for judging a horse is that it should be short above and long below — that is, it should have a short span from the withers to the hips, but as long a span as possible from the hindquarters to the forequarters — and it should besides have sound feet.
A good hoof, then—

—for a good horse’s leg is light and easy to lift, and neither too broad nor too high, and has little flesh but a thick horn. A good hoof also gives evidence of itself by its sound: for the hollow hoof rings like a cymbal more than the full, fleshy one. Let the pastern be supple, and let the horse not be a ‘dog-walker.’ Let it have bony shins, and let the parts around the fibula and the shin be lean, sinewy, and as free of flesh as possible up to the knee, while the parts above this should be fleshier and stronger.

Let the space between the legs be as wide as possible; for this will let it throw its legs forward with the longest stride. Let the chest be neither too narrow nor too broad, and the shoulder-blade as large and broad as possible, and the armpit small. Let the neck and the forequarters stand upright, the growth not curving back toward the withers, and let the withers be as thick and broad as possible. Beside the jaw let the neck be slender and supple, curving back toward the poll, but then bending forward again from its slenderest point.

And let it carry the head forward, and let the neck not be short, and let the crest be high, and let the head be very distinctive and light. Let the nostrils be as large as possible, and the jowls not thick, and matching each other evenly. Let the eyes be large, set as far out as possible, and bright to look at; the ears small, and the teeth and the jaw as small as possible,
and let the parts between the neck and the jaw be as loose and supple as possible,

and let the withers be as high as possible, and the back, and let the ribs be as broad as possible and set low down, and let the loins be supple (one could recognize suppleness if the horse does not stand evenly on both legs, but for the most part shifts its weight onto one of its hind legs), and the haunch as large and broad as possible, and the flank as small as possible. The ribs themselves should be broad, and the haunch large, but the jaw the smallest and weakest part of the horse.

The thighs should not be fleshy, and the testicles should be small. The space between the thighs should be neither too high nor too full, but somewhat close together, and the anus as small as possible and set as far back as possible from view. Let the tail be carried high, and thick and long from the haunches.

So much, then, for the appearance of horses; and the horse that has all these qualities to the highest degree is best, and second is the one that has most of them. For the more of these qualities it possesses, the greater the benefits it provides.

A foal is weaned from the herd of young foals at two years old. Around this time, having reached thirty months, it sheds its first teeth, the second a year later, and the last in another year, in a shorter time still. It reaches its own peak in speed and boldness of action at six years old.
Theomnestus, on the selection of a horse. Let us first say a few words about what sort of horse the one making the—
—choice of a mature horse ought to be. It should therefore be strong and handsome.

Now a horse’s strength lies in its feet, and its beauty in its head. For it is in these parts first that its strength and beauty are shown. We shall judge its strength both from the place where it was born and from its gait.

From its place of origin: when it is a mountain horse, from rocky mountain country, born of a sire of the same kind. For horses can also be weak-footed by breed, whenever mountain mares are covered by stallions not themselves from the mountains, through the deposit of seed. This weakness is hereditary, as with men who suffer from foot-gout, and as with grey-eyed horses. One must, then, pay attention not only to the places where the horses themselves were born, but also to their sires and dams, lest marsh-bred mares be covered by mountain stallions.

In general, one judges from the gait and the set of the hoof — when it happens to be thick, upright, rather narrow, and hollow underneath. Now the other signs — the thickness of the hoof, its narrowness, its uprightness — are recognizable simply by looking; but whether it is hollow underneath, we shall know quickly from the gait. For the horse with a hollow hoof gives a certain cymbal-like ring to the ears of those listening as it strikes level ground, and this ring proclaims the horse to be the stronger. The cause of this, I believe, is as follows: there is a piece of flesh, gristly and cartilaginous, projecting beyond the rim and hidden within it, triangular in shape, to which—

—the ends of the coronet of the hoof are said to be attached near the pastern-joint, as though girded by it. If, then, horses that are soft and weak in the feet wear down their hooves on journeys and rough ground, the coronet draws near to the ground. This part is where the sinews terminate, and spasm and fever set in, and, if not treated, the animal dies. For this reason such a horse should not be given up on, but cared for.

As for beauty, to put it briefly, it lies in the horse’s body being neither too large nor too small: a smaller head — for so it will neither look downward, and will be proud, having a small, light head held high in the air. Let the whole body be lean, with the skin not pressed tight against the bones, and let the veins, not being hidden beneath the flesh of the body, be plainly visible.

A broader forehead, a narrower nose, gently curved, nostrils wide open, so that it may breathe in and out easily. A mouth-opening proportionate in size to the mouth, ending in a somewhat pointed and hairless shape; a shaggy, large mouth-opening is sluggish and donkey-like.

A large eye, prominent, and as though starting from its socket — for a horse with such an eye is ready for movement. Let it have a neck matching its head, beginning narrow, but rising gracefully and in proportion to its size, like a rooster’s. Let the mane fall along the neck: if double, let it go unclipped; if single-maned, let it be clipped close, showing off the bare beauty of the neck through the clipping.
Let it have a double, rounded—

—breast, shins running down lean and free of excess hair, an ankle not thick, so that it is not heavy-footed. Let the ‘dog-pastern’ at the ankle be neither too great nor too small a span: for the elongated, narrow kind is prone to injury in the lifting of leaps, while the very small kind, being close to the coronet of the hoof, becomes ulcerated from chafing in running. In addition, let it have a double spine, so that on either side of it the rising of the loin muscles makes the spine-bearing bone appear hollow. Let it have firm ribs, set low at the flank, and let the flank be drawn forward. Let the thighs be well rounded, and let the muscles, both above and below, stand out with a hollow in the middle. Let the hocks be lean, sinewy, not loose, the groins inside the thighs rounded like a ball, so that the bulging outline of the muscles, both outer and inner, straightens the thigh-bone, which tends to be bowed. Let the foot have a length greater than its height. Let the tail be moderately haired, its origin at the outset not showing. These, then, are the marks of strength and beauty.

The marks of spiritedness of temperament are these: let the foal in the herd not always stay close to its mother, but leap and bound like a gazelle, boldly clear enclosures, jump ditches fearlessly, and disregard the danger of rivers. For these are qualities natural to foals. When full-grown, let it be good-humored, ready for running, quick to be reined in, not one-sided in the mouth nor a rearer — for these are marks of cowardice and viciousness. Let it not sweat quickly, for this is a mark of being out of condition; let it accept the bit—

—willingly, for such a horse is eager for exertion. Having received it, let it chew and send foam from its mouth — for this is the sign of a spirited horse. Let it not stand still under a blow, but leap toward the whistle. Let it snort while running — for it finds relief by expelling the breath produced by motion and taking in clean air instead, since it is naturally strengthened by being nourished on this. Let it accept the rider readily, for a horse that does not do this is clearly treacherous. Let it recognize its trainer, and, if he approaches, let it neigh — for these are marks of affection and trustworthiness.

How, then, one ought to care for such a horse, and when, it would now be timely to teach you. It is better to begin breaking a horse in summer and autumn. For the green fodder, being abundant, is familiar food to foals, and, once accustomed, it will offset the exhaustion of exercise, being made unfamiliar with only the one thing — being put to work — while the weather in both seasons has neither drought nor frost. For drought makes the foal too dry and causes illness, while frost, chilling the foal as it sweats from exercise, produces stiffness, and further brings on a cough from chilling.

For when the mouth is parted from the bit and the throat is exposed to the blowing of the winds, the depths of the throat are chilled and dried out, and this condition results in coughing as a symptom. It seems better to me that the well-bred foal, raised by a careful horse-breeder, should be kept with its mother, feeding at the manger. For, becoming accustomed to men
from a young age and thus becoming tame, it will in time, through the habit of familiarity, be tamed — not subdued by the force of a hobble.

Every foal should accept the bit at not less than eighteen months old, and should be handled by hand in its simple, gentle nature. The one currying the foal should begin, as though scratching it, from the head and the chin, for these are the parts the foal most enjoys having scratched by its trainer. Since it cannot easily scratch these places itself, when the one currying it does so most pleasingly, it stretches out its neck on its own. The currying should proceed downward from above, and likewise the cleaning of the shed hairs. For in this way the parts already groomed remain clean, while those not yet groomed will be cleaned without soiling what has already been cleaned.

Next, in order, the shoulders, shoulder-blades, ribs, and flanks — but let him not go abruptly from the flank to the groin. For the animal is especially ticklish, as they say, in this place. But, if it grows fond of it through habit, he may bring his hand there too, provided he does not startle it — or rather, having begun, let him continue rubbing it. Some foals, when rubbed on the feet, are accustomed, from a mixture of pleasure and numbness, to crouch down and sometimes to urinate.

If it does this, so that it does not become habituated to the reaction, one must either whip it gently with a rod or with a thin strap of raw hide. For the pain of the blow dulls the numbness arising from pleasure, making it weaker.
After the groin, let him move his hands to the back, and, going down, to the round joints, the hocks, the muscles, and the hind shins.

Then, taking hold of the tail, let him bring it around through the hind legs, and, drawing it out to the flank, wind it with his left hand as far as beyond the hair, and, pressing it against the hip-socket itself, bringing his right hand more firmly to the pastern-space, let him rub it this way, drawing it up and bending the hind leg toward the flank. For by doing this he will neither be kicked, and will make the foal more ready to lift its hind foot. [Pressing the left hand against the hip-socket.]

This maneuver of bringing the tail through the hind legs to the flanks will prevent the foal from kicking with both feet at once. For it is impossible for a horse or other draught animal to kick with both feet together before first raising its tail high. Having thus secured himself beforehand, once he has accustomed the feet, let the trainer trim around the hooves, so that, if there is any bruise anywhere, the trainer, by cleaning it, may discover it and the foal may be treated. After currying the foal, let him gently and gradually raise its leg, accustoming it little by little — but not too forcefully, even once it becomes accustomed, let him raise it high — so that it does not become distressed by being forced.

It is especially at this time that one must fasten and pay attention to the cheek-strap, that is, the chin-strap; for the browband often tends to twist over onto the eyes, and, if this happens, it either chafes and ulcerates the eye, or, tearing the membrane, blinds it.
After hanging up its food for no more than one hour, one should lead it to the river, and, after watering it, begin to feed it on rather soft fodder, that is—

—oats. For oats are milk-like and easily digested, and have a husk around the grain, and for this reason the foal is not made too unfamiliar with taking it in. Let it eat three ounces in the first month, six in the second, nine in the third, eighteen in the fourth, until it completes its second year. For then it must be introduced to barley too, and eat more.

Then, in turn, it accepts a rider on its shoulders. For before two years old I forbid a rider to mount a foal. For its back suffers from the weight, and often the spine, being still soft, is bent, and thereafter such a horse becomes useless, or develops a sway-back. First a light boy should leap onto the foal. After thirty full months, it should accept a grown rider and be given more abundant food and more exercise.

Let the measure of food be no more than twenty-five and a half ounces. For eating too much food, even if it does not harm at once, settles in the feet and ruins the hooves through excess raw matter. So much, then, for recognizing and caring for a foal.

How one must know a horse’s age. Horses are required in all equestrian contests from five to twenty years of age, as many have said, but for everyday use they are needed by careful owners from two years old up to their thirtieth year. The sign of age, then, changes along with bodily growth. For when it is two years and six months old, it sheds half its teeth, that is, those of the upper part. When it reaches four years,
—it sheds its canine teeth, and these change within six years. As the molars fall out, then, it replaces those it has lost, and, having reached seven years, having completed them all, it is now full.

And from this time on it has teeth that are hollowed. Henceforth, then, one can no longer tell how many years old it is, except from someone else’s testimony.
