For nature has also granted signs and marks of age in the bodily features, which we recognize better by sight than we can convey in writing. For in its tenth year, the temples begin to hollow, and the eyebrows for the most part turn grey; moreover, the teeth also protrude. In its twelfth year a certain blackness appears between the teeth.

For horses that are kept indoors and led by bits, careful attention recognizes the years. For the wrinkles of their lips reveal this: indeed, counting the wrinkles beginning from the mouth, you will find from them the years of the animal. But for an untamed horse it is difficult to find the years.

On the number of the veins. Following on from this, one must also state the number of the veins: in the palate, two veins; at the temples, two; under the eyes, two [lacuna]; and from the coronets, four; and from the [lacuna], four; from the fetlock, two; from the thighs, two; under the hocks, two; and from the tail, one — so that the veins together come to twenty-nine.
On the lifespan of horses. The Persians’ horses have a long span of years; the Huns’, the Epirotes’, and the—

—Sicilians’ a shorter one. But for Spanish horses and those of the Nosemi, there is a persistent assumption that barbarian horses should be given no help by way of drenching at all, since, by the great benefit of their nature, the sick ones among them recover on their own, so that care actually harms them. But this assumption is false. For the stronger their bodies are, the longer they live — provided the treatment given by the art is not lacking.

On phlebotomy of geldings. It is nevertheless demonstrated by the writers that blood should never be drawn from the principal vein of geldings, except perhaps in case of great and extreme necessity. This is because they lost the greatest part of their natural heat along with their testicles. But from the palate — provided negligence does not prevent it — in nearly every month, blood must be reduced, both for geldings and for those still possessing their testicles. Stallions, if not restrained, are often said to go blind. In that year in which a stallion is used for breeding, one must not draw its blood, lest the exertion of the double demand, with the body already strained by breeding, exhaust it.
Concerning the care of horses, of their stables, and the rest, the first and second books will explain.
On the training of war-horses and on breaking-in.
On starvation of horses and draught animals, and for every animal that is sick or starving.
On indigestion. Grind salt with pellitory and
marjoram, pour on an equal amount of mixed wine, and drench.

A morsel for a horse. Three ounces of myrrh from the Troglodyte country, one ounce of cardamom, one and a half ounces of linseed, one and a half ounces each of raisins and pine-nuts, two pounds three ounces of honey.
On displacement of the bladder.
For frost-stroke.
On ileus. For retention of the belly. Three ounces of oil, niter, five eggs, four ounces of warm water; inject into the rectum with a clyster.

On the mulberry-sore. Another way — this also works on humans, and saves them. Smear the affliction with honey from the comb, or sprinkle on orpiment and resin, or anoint with orpiment and honey and sprinkle on top burnt dog’s-head, or make an effective ointment with fish-sauce and a little warm water, and anoint repeatedly, until it withers away. Or chop mulberry-tree leaves small, mix them into the feed, and give; or anoint continually with the first-run of soap, until it withers away.
A plaster for the ring-growth and the mulberry-sore. Take up equal parts of soap and lime, pepper and salt, and bandage on.

For the mulberry-sore. Cleanse the place with old wine and sprinkle on split orpiment three times a day, and it will heal; or grind Gangra salt and chewed walnut together — let the salt be the lesser part — and, having washed the wound well, apply repeatedly with a linen cloth. As for the so-called ‘female’ mulberry-sore, considered by some incurable, you will cure it if you anoint it with blood
taken from a woman’s menstrual flow. Or take fresh, well-sifted quicklime, split orpiment, garlic, and pepper, combine and knead them, and apply, and leave it until the same hour the next day.
[lacuna] Do not undo this until it is drawn up and falls away. But if the wound is large and protruding, bandage it with raw silk-cotton, and, anointing from above with the remedy, bind it.
On fistula.

A useful remedy for those troubled by fistula is the cautery. But if the wound is raised above the surface, first shave around it and clean away the unsound, raised tissue, then apply red-hot cauteries, so as to cut away the affected parts and leave it clean. Then use the remedy made with the green ointment. The vetch-and-honey mixture applied as a poultice is also fitting, especially for those with a persistent discharge and those infested with worms.
Another way. Take up equal parts of myrrh, aloe, frankincense, and pomegranate rind with bull’s gall, and use. Others also flush fistulas with cedar-resin, and succeed marvelously.

Another way. Since sinuses badly treated tend to become fistulous, it follows that we should speak of fistulas. The fistula is so named by metaphor from the pipes made of reed or some other material: for a certain wide hollow space is found, similar to the cavities in reeds. The sinus, once it has become calloused, cannot be treated without surgery or a strong medication. As for the oblique fistulas that run beneath the skin, we relieve
—the skin, cutting it open along its whole length in a straight incision
down to the calluses that are the cause of the fistula. If they are near the surface, we scrape them away with the edge of the scalpel.

But if the calloused tissue lies deep, we remove it entirely. For unless such tissue is removed, neither new flesh can grow nor can the sores scar over. And if the shape of the fistula is not oblique, but the opposite — that is, running deep — we remove the fistula in a circle, cutting away as much of the surrounding flesh as is needed so that the calluses are completely excised.
And if the fistula ends at a bone, once the bones are exposed we scrape them down to a scale’s thickness. After removing the calloused tissue, we treat it as the other sores are treated.
A remedy of Oribasius for fistula, that removes calluses even from old fistulas.

Equal parts of blue vitriol, copper ore, raw chalcitis, verdigris, split alum, Sinopian red ochre, and gum, chopped separately, taken up with vinegar and frankincense; make into an eye-salve-like preparation and use. For it clears away the calloused parts of sinuses, and, mixed with honey, builds flesh and closes the scar.
Another useful remedy that cleanses fistulas from within. It works excellently also for headache, bruised ears, and dysentery sufferers, and dries up all moisture.

Grind snail flesh with the shells, small bulbs, asphalt, aloe, and frankincense in equal parts with vinegar and apply as a poultice. Or use two ounces of aloe and alkanet root dry. For it fills in and closes the scar.

An unfailing eye-salve for fistula, called ‘Heracles.’ It also removes fistulas of the eye. First insert papyrus into the fistula down to its roots for one day, and, to the measure of the fistula — that is, of the papyrus — insert the eye-salve, and leave it for three days. On the fourth, undo it, and you will find the fistula opened up entirely. It is made thus: four and a half hexagia of shell-shaped cadmia, three hexagia eighteen carats of burnt copper, one ounce of roasted copper ore, one ounce of roasted chalcitis, four and a half hexagia of blue vitriol, seven blister-beetles by number, eighteen carats of dry frankincense-resin, one whole root of autumn crocus, gum one and a half hexagia; taking it up with vinegar, make it into various eye-salves and use.

On fistulas, that is, tumors that form on the animal, which the barbarians call ‘sklepaditzas.’ If that part begins to produce swellings, the body shivers from the swellings themselves and becomes fistulous imperceptibly. At that point it also droops its eyes and has its ears hanging loose. One must therefore treat it thus: if the swellings show themselves in whatever place, cauterize them at once, down to the living flesh, so that the little fistulas feel the cautery. Such a fistula is like a green gourd, and, inserting a probe or the flat of a probe from any direction, it passes right through, and the animal feels no pain. Cut, so that with a cauterizing instrument you excise the same place down to the living tissue. One should note that this affliction tends to take hold especially in the forward parts of the horse, because it more easily—
—than the hind parts can be treated; for the hind ones offer no hope of survival. Bind up this fistula with linen soaked in oil and vinegar. Many apply linen soaked in urine and lard instead.
For those discharging moisture from the nostrils, and if the nasal cartilage should split and cause bleeding.
A nasal remedy for hemorrhage. Pour in coriander juice.

Hierocles’s remedy for the same. Pitch a sponge, and so on; or very cold water, and so on; or heat a millstone-fragment red-hot and quench it in very sharp vinegar, and bring the vapor to the nostrils, and the flow will be stopped.
On empyema.

On empyema: prognosis and cure. The horse hangs its head, breathes heavily, wastes away, cannot hold down drink, shivers about the nostrils, and has a foul smell from the mouth, and when it rolls it does not roll all the way over, and, wanting to cough, cannot. It is treated thus: boil a cock and a puppy together, and, once the sinews of both have dissolved, pour off the broth and remove the bones and sinews. Discard the flesh, but keep the brain, and add to the broth five ounces of myrrh, three ounces of cassia, about a handful of poppy seed, and four and a half ounces of oil; strain it, and, opening the mouth as little as possible, give it warm. Feed it on green fodder; if dry, sprinkle it with water, and drench again every fifth day, up to a third time. Also give hulled barley, and let it walk about covered with a blanket.
On horses with poor appetite and distaste for food.
On horses with poor appetite and distaste for food.

When a horse swallows whole barley grains, its body wastes correspondingly and its gums become inflamed, and saliva flows more continuously. It is treated thus: mix chalky earth with very sharp vinegar, and apply it warm to the jaws for six days, and three times a day rub its gums with honey and pomegranate rind.
If a horse loses its appetite in summer. Grind tragacanth, myrrh, saffron, Illyrian iris, frankincense meal, feverfew, ground-pine, and spurge-laurel with milk, and drench.
Instruction on caustic, that is, cauterizing agents.

Instruction on caustic, that is, cauterizing agents. We use the substances called caustic, or cauterizing, on calloused excess growths and sometimes on cancerous sores, and on scrofulous swellings, when we wish to cause them to slough, and on hip and joint afflictions. We apply these in place of the cautery on ant-warts, skin-tags, corns, and fig-like growths. But their greatest use is on carbuncle-like and malignant sores. For, applied to these, they check the spreading sore and, causing the scabs to fall off, deliver the patient from danger most quickly.
A non-biting caustic. Half an ounce of scale, one and a half hexagia of realgar, eighteen carats each of black hellebore and orpiment. Some use split alum instead of the orpiment.
Another non-biting caustic that penetrates deeply. One hexagion six carats each of scale and realgar, eighteen carats of black hellebore. On moist sores use it—
—dry; on others, dissolved in rose oil, for it is good that way.
Another very effective astringent caustic. Grind safflower seed, red scale, and realgar in equal parts, and use with rose oil.
On colic sufferers, that is, those with pain in the colon.

On colic, and how it will be recognized. The head droops toward the ground, and it drags its legs, throws itself to the ground and rises again. Sweat breaks out about the armpits; it flees from the pain, unable to bear the inflammation. At other times it throws itself down and lies on its back, stretching its head back and its legs straight up, and sometimes it arches over even further and rolls about, and turns its gaze toward its flank, showing the aching place, betrayed by the inflammation, grinding its teeth and groaning, and striking the ground with its feet, unable to endure the pains.
As the affliction intensifies, the horse does not easily recover. It is relieved thus: roast donkey’s milk and cress with dark wine and give it.
If a draught animal is found, upon palpation, to have swelling along its flank.

One ounce of resin, nine ounces of sifted barley meal, nine ounces of wax, enough very sharp vinegar. Boil the vinegar first, then add the meal, stirring carefully so that it does not scorch. Then add the resin and the rest, and apply warm, wrapped in wool, for three days.
On prolapse of the rectum. Foment the rectum with a decoction of cyclamen or white hellebore.
An antidote for colic that works the same day, given during attacks, painlessly—

—the size of a Pontic walnut with water. Two ounces each of henbane and white pepper, four hexagia of Cretan wild-carrot, one ounce four hexagia of opium, one hexagion of spelt grain, one hexagion each of saffron, spurge, spikenard, and pellitory; take it up with honey and, kneading it thoroughly, use.
By Africanus. Against Cycnus’s affliction: the right testicle worn as an amulet stops the disease.
On the swallowing of bones.
For dracontia.
On various diseases and their treatments, and on the removal of thorns and on brand-marks.

On the removal of a thorn. The tenderest root of the reed, ground in a mortar, taken up with honey, and brought to the consistency of a wax-salve, spread on linen and applied, draws a thorn out of the flesh. For if it is left on through the whole night, in the morning you will find the thorns stuck to the remedy.

For soaking mixed grains. Seven parts each of barley and oats, three of chickpea, three of vetch, twenty of bitter vetch, five of grass-pea, twenty of lentil-vetch, ten of lentil, five of fenugreek, ten of broad bean, ten of wheat; mix and store, and give each horse seven parts daily.
Another way, for the good disposition of dumb animals. Wear the root of the cinquefoil plant along with the name of Jesus Christ as an amulet.

On preventing animals from falling sick. Chop a piece of stag’s antler and give each animal one to wear as an amulet. Or boil fennel root or the plant called ‘sacred herb’ and anoint the head, forehead, and neck—

—or two ounces each of opopanax and castoreum, one ounce of galbanum, two ounces each of turpentine, butter, Bruttian pitch, and resin, one ounce each of white wax, lard, henna oil, and bay oil; mix, take it up, and use as a fumigation. Or fumigate the manger and the dumb animals with stag horn.

By Africanus, so that horses are not startled or spooked on the road. Horses being needlessly startled, or thrown into confusion by empty sights or shadows, will be stopped if a wolf’s tail, cut from the living beast, is fastened to the animal’s right ear.
So that a donkey does not fall on the road. Pull hairs from its tail and tie them to its teeth, and it will not fall.

On ampelos. If a horse or other draught animal develops ampelos, purulent varicose swellings will form around it. One must treat these with the cautery, applying it upright to each one of the pus-filled swellings, and anointing with the ointment, until the scabs fall off.

By Africanus, the removal of brand-marks from horses. This is a theft practiced on valuable horses: to alter their brands, remove and erase the letters burned into their bodies, and, with a different coloring, make the former mark unrecognizable to its previous owner. It is done thus: a pulse, whose kind is inscribed at the end under the seventh hexagion, cooked at the new moon in the third hour, is applied by dipping the part you wish to erase into it. For, having caused an ulcer through the burning, it brings up white hair. And if you apply it in several places, what was formerly a single color will become multicolored.
In every case, for all colors other than white alone (excepted because of how similarly the growing hair matches it), the technique will erase the mark but preserve the original color.

To make a mark on horses without a cautery. Make an ash of equal parts of light pumice, sea-snail shells, white niter, fig leaves, and burnt beans; shave the place and sprinkle on vinegar, letting it drip, and rub well twice a day, until the place is bare. Then draw whatever mark you wish, and, taking unripe oak-galls, alum, sumac, verdigris of copper and of silver, and blue vitriol, grind them all equally, letting vinegar drip in. And, making it to the thickness of a soft wax-salve, and having first touched it with liquid alum in the
evening, paint on whatever mark you wish. The next day, having rubbed it off thoroughly, paint it on again, for six days. Then wash it off with old urine, and the mark will hold well.
On the preparation of drenches.
Another. Hyssop, and so on; enough tragacanth, half an ounce of fennel, one ounce each of rose oil and marjoram, one and a half ounces of honey, enough wine.
A purgative drench. One ounce each of centaury and niter, three ounces of hog’s fennel, five ounces each of colocynth and peony, two pounds four ounces of wine; drench for three days in succession.

For the health of the animal. Two ounces each of lovage and pepper, one and a half ounces each of spelt grain, saffron, oil, and sulphur, one ounce of honey; mix, sprinkle around, and drench with these.
For chilling. Four and a half hexagia of saffron, myrrh, cost—

—us, two and a half ounces each, cassia two and a half ounces, cardamom three ounces, malabathrum leaf five ounces, Illyrian iris four and a half hexagia, asarum four ounces, melilot one ounce, tragacanth two ounces, pepper one ounce, enough old wine and unripe-olive oil, egg white, one ounce of honey; drench for several days.

A purgative remedy for herd animals. Since it is not possible to take hold of pastured mares continually by hand, one must purge them with this preventive remedy in spring and autumn, and they will not quickly fall into mange or disease. I therefore recommend this excellent remedy, than which there is none better: chop wild-cucumber root, mix in niter and a third part of salt, and drench them and give it to eat. By this the foals too are purged, through the milk of the mature mares. One must also purge the tame ones when they are sent out to green pasture, so that it may cleanse at the same time the ill humor left from their old fodder.
The preparation of a barley-cake for every kind of disease.

Illyrian iris, long birthwort, gentian, bear’s-foot, myrrh, chickpea flour, hyssop, Gallic garlic, southernwood, parsley, and celery seed, one ounce each, eight grains of pepper; boil with wine and honey, and give three ounces to each animal for three days.
The preparation of the bitter remedy. [the manuscript breaks off here, unfinished]
